title: Architecture Patterns and Low-Level Design
description: Architecture patterns and low-level design: SOLID, design patterns, domain-driven design and low-level system design.
objectives: Apply SOLID where it pays and ignore it where it does not
Turn a vague requirement into modular components with clear boundaries
Explain why one design beats its alternatives

practice.title: Scenario 1 — The DataManager that does everything
items: Difficulty
The design
Defects, worst first
No seam anywhere. Nothing is testable without a live database and a network. This is the root cause of the other problems.
Singleton global state. Test pollution, hidden dependencies, thread/request safety, a lifecycle the container should own.
Divergent change. Every feature change edits this one file; every release conflicts with every other.
Business logic and I/O interleaved. You cannot unit test a pricing rule because it is three lines above a db.query.
Tangled change. A logging change and a checkout change both land here.
The fix, in order
Characterisation tests on the three highest-value operations *before* touching anything.
Wrap the payment and email calls behind ports (PaymentGateway, Notifier) so they can be faked. Two-line changes, huge payoff.
Split by capability: OrderRepository, PaymentGateway, EmailSender, PricingRule.
Inject the clock, the logger and the cache instead of using statics.
Move business rules into domain objects; leave the repositories as data access.
Replace the singleton with a composition root (buildContainer(env)) so lifetimes and test doubles are explicit.
Do not rewrite. Strangler Fig: extract one capability per sprint.
Ask the team first

practice.title: Scenario 2 — Order processing with a God service and no transactions
items: Difficulty
The design
Defects, worst first
No timeouts on 6 remote calls. A single slow dependency saturates the request path. This is the single highest-severity defect and it is a five-minute fix.
Cross-service partial failure is unhandled. payment failed → continue means orders exist with no payment and nobody knows.
Fan-out latency. 6 sequential calls add up; Promise.all where they are independent.
State in three databases with no saga. No consistency story, no compensation, no reconciliation.
14 dependencies = a God service by injection count alone. Nobody can test it without 14 doubles.
The fix
Timeout every call with a nested budget (inner deadline < outer deadline). Add retries with jitter on idempotent reads only, and a budget that fits inside the caller's deadline.
Per-dependency circuit breakers + bulkheads so one failure cannot consume everything.

Make the payment step a saga step with compensation; anything that must not fail the order is inside the saga, anything optional (notifications, analytics) is emitted as an event and leaves the critical path.
Parallelise independent calls; the pricing call does not need inventory.
Split the service by capability; the fraud engine and the notification sender do not belong in one unit.
Read-side fan-out: for the order page, a read model or a BFF, so 6 calls happen on the read path with per-field degradation rather than in the write path.
Ask the team first

practice.title: Scenario 3 — Event bus with 14 subscribers and no contracts
items: Difficulty
The design
Defects, worst first
The business flow lives in subscribers. Nobody can answer "what happens after order.placed?" That is 9 files and no single reading order.
No unsubscribe → listeners leak; long-lived subscribers capture request scope.
Mutable payloads shared across subscribers: subscriber 3 mutates the entity that subscriber 7 sees.
Errors swallowed → a broken subscriber is invisible for weeks.
Stringly typed → a renamed field is a runtime no-op in one subscriber and a live bug in another.
No idempotency → at-least-once delivery causes duplicate charges, duplicate shipments.
The fix
Name the critical path as an explicit orchestrator (an application service or a saga) and keep only non-critical reactions as events.
Typed event map + readonly/frozen payloads.
Per-listener error isolation with a metric; aggregate failures; alert.
on() returns a disposer; wire it to lifecycle (onRequestEnd, onUnmount, dispose).
Idempotent handlers keyed on eventId with a unique constraint.
Version the event names and add a tolerant-reader contract test in CI.
Consider Promise.allSettled semantics for async listeners instead of fire-and-forget.
Ask the team first

practice.title: Scenario 4 — Repository that leaks the ORM
items: Difficulty
The design
Defects, worst first
The interface is not a domain abstraction — it is a thin wrapper over the ORM, with the ORM in the signature. Nothing can be faked without a DB.
N+1 everywhere, because services write joins by hand.
The ORM entity is the API response, so internal fields (password hash, internal flags, soft-delete columns) leak and the API cannot be shaped for a client.
Lazy loading ⇒ detached-object exceptions and surprise queries during serialisation.
No explicit loading ⇒ transactions leak into read paths.
The fix

Domain-named methods: findOpenOrdersForCustomer(customerId): Promise<Order[]>, byId(id): Promise<Order | null>. Kill findByCustomerId(status?, from?) — every parameter combination is a new method or a spec object.
A OrderMapper for row ⇄ domain, and a separate OrderView DTO for the API.
Explicit loading inside the repository (one join, one round trip) so N+1 is impossible by construction.
Strict validation on hydration; unknown enum values are a data-integrity error, not a cast.
Add a version column and optimistic concurrency in save.
Ask the team first

practice.title: Scenario 5 — Microservices with a shared database
items: Difficulty
The design
Defects, worst first
Distributed monolith: all the cost, none of the benefit. The coordinated deploy proves it.
Shared schema is a hidden synchronous coupling: you cannot migrate a column without coordinating everyone; you cannot extract a service later because its data is shared.
Data ownership is fiction. Every service is coupled to every table change.
Local calls that used to be free now cost latency and can fail — with none of the resilience patterns applied because "it's just SQL".
Operational overhead without isolation: 9 pipelines, 9 dashboards, 9 on-call rotations, zero fault isolation.
The fix, in order
Admit the problem: this is a monolith with extra processes. Decide honestly whether to (a) merge back to a modular monolith or (b) complete the split.
Establish data ownership: each service owns its tables; others go through APIs or replicated read models.
Sequence the data split with an expand/migrate/contract plan (add the new structure, dual-write, backfill, verify, cut reads, remove the old).
Replace cross-service table reads with a read model for the pages that genuinely need joined data, and with events for replication.
Add the resilience patterns (timeouts, breakers, bulkheads, idempotency) because the calls are now remote.
Unblock independent deploys: backward-compatible contracts and a one-service-at-a-time release train.
Ask the team first

practice.title: Scenario 6 — Anemic domain model in a complex billing system
items: Difficulty
The design
Defects, worst first
Invalid states are representable and reachable — an invoice with status: VOID and total > 0 exists in production (or will).
Rule drift across 6 services; the 6th copy is wrong and nobody knows which is authoritative.
No reuse: a new entry point (CLI, webhook, job) re-implements the rules a 7th time.
Transaction sprawl: 40 service methods, each managing its own boundaries, so multi-step operations are not atomic.
The service class is a 3,000-line God object (SRP violated from every direction).
The fix
Move the rules into behaviour on the entity: invoice.finalize(now), invoice.void(reason), invoice.applyCreditNote(amount), each rejecting illegal transitions.
Make fields private with intent-revealing accessors; the invariant is enforced in one place.
Delete the duplicated guards from the services; keep the *use-case policy* (who may void an invoice, in which role) in the service, where it belongs.
Introduce a Money value object so money cannot be a number.
Wrap the use case in an application service that owns the transaction; one use case per method.
Enforce with tests at both levels: domain tests (rules) and one integration test per use case.
Ask the team first

practice.title: Scenario 7 — Rate limiter that blocks on a slow store
items: Difficulty
The design
Defects, worst first
Check-then-increment race → over-admission under exactly the conditions you care about (a stampede at the limit).
Synchronous dependency in the hot path with no timeout → Redis latency becomes request latency; a Redis blip becomes a site outage.
Unbounded key space with no TTL → memory exhaustion (the limiter becomes the outage vector).
Fails closed implicitly (throws) with no local fallback → total outage on a limiter failure.
Missing Retry-After/X-RateLimit-* → clients hammer in a tight loop.
The fix
Move prune/count/compare/increment into one Lua script (or an atomic pipeline) — indivisible.
Wrap the store call in a timeout; fail open to a local token bucket when the store is unavailable, and alert on it. (Or fail closed for billing quotas — decide and document.)
Set a TTL on every key and/or cap the tracked key space; add idle eviction in the local limiter.
Return 429 with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset.
Consider rate limiting at the edge (gateway/CDN) so over-limit traffic never reaches the app.
Instrument: allowed/rejected per key class, store latency, fallback rate; alert on rejection spikes (a DDoS signal).
Ask the team first

practice.title: Scenario 8 — "Microservices" with 200 nanosecond network calls
items: Difficulty
The design
Defects, worst first
7 round trips on the critical path from a mobile client; latency and failure probability compound. At 99.9% per call, all 7 succeeding is ~99.3%.
No failure isolation: one slow service degrades the whole page with no partial rendering.
API surface leaks the service topology — every internal split becomes a client-breaking change.
Over-fetching: the mobile client downloads desktop-shaped payloads.
No per-client authorisation or shaping.
The fix
Introduce a BFF per channel (web-bff, mobile-bff): one call, payload shaped for the client.
Inside the BFF, Promise.all with a per-call timeout, a circuit breaker, and a per-field fallback so a broken service degrades one card, not the page.
Add an aggregate cache with per-field TTLs and single-flight coalescing so 40 concurrent requests for one SKU make one upstream call.
Define a page latency budget and enforce it: each upstream gets a share; slow ones are abandoned early.
Cache popular aggregates at the edge/CDN for the marketing pages.
Keep authorisation in the services; use the BFF only for channel-specific shaping and coarse session checks. Never trust a client-supplied user id.
Ask the team first

practice.title: Scenario 9 — Service mesh adopted too early
items: Difficulty
The design
Defects, worst first
Retry amplification — mesh retries × client retries × LB retries can produce a 10× load multiplier during an incident, which is the opposite of the goal.
Retry on non-idempotent methods in mesh config → duplicate writes.
No capacity for the data plane: sidecar CPU/memory unset → noisy-neighbour problems.
The control plane is now an operational dependency; readiness without holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts means pods get no traffic after rollout.
Debugging cost is high and the team cannot pay it — mesh config is not covered by their tests.
Value is not being realised: no canary-by-header, no mTLS enforcement yet, and the underlying problem was application design.
The fix
Do the resilience work in code for now: timeouts, breakers, bulkheads, retries with jitter and budgets, idempotency. They are testable there, and there are only 6 services.
If the mesh stays: disable mesh retries entirely; keep exactly one retry layer.
Restrict retries to idempotent verbs; ensure idempotency keys on writes.
Set sidecar resource requests/limits; configure outlier detection and connection draining to survive rolling deploys.
Move to STRICT mTLS deliberately, and check holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts.
GitOps the mesh config with review; add mesh-version to the app version in dashboards.
Plan the exit: decide the threshold (services, teams, compliance need) under which you remove it, and write it down.
Ask the team first

practice.title: Scenario 10 — Serverless with a connection pool per invocation
items: Difficulty
The design
Defects, worst first
Connection storm: 1,000 concurrent invocations × 10 connections = 10,000 connections against a limit of ~200. The database is the outage cause.
No timeouts on downstream calls → cold starts plus unbounded latency; no init-duration visibility.
Batch failures are all-or-nothing: one poison message fails the batch and 9 good messages are retried forever.
Retries without a DLQ and without idempotency → duplicate processing, unbounded cost.
No concurrency cap, so a queue burst instantiates unbounded handlers and amplifies the DB problem.
Cold start is blamed, but the real cost is connection initialisation per invocation.
The fix
Module-scope pool (reused per warm container) sized to db_max_connections × share; or RDS Proxy/PgBouncer; or front the function with a queue with bounded concurrency.
Batched DB access; a single query or a batch API instead of per-row queries.
Handle each record in a batch independently and return batchItemFailures; DLQ the poison message with the payload and error.
Reserved concurrency per function to protect downstream dependencies; a per-user rate limit if fan-out is unbounded.
Explicit timeout on every downstream call; instrument Init Duration separately from handler duration.
Move long-running work out of the function; use a worker for anything beyond the timeout.
Thin handler + reusable core module (the B pattern from 11.3.9).
Ask the team first

practice.title: Scenario 11 — A Strategy that is a switch in disguise
items: Difficulty
The design
Defects, worst first
The decision is still in one place and is still closed to extension. Adding a segment edits the factory. This is the *entire* cost of Strategy with none of the benefit.
The algorithms are not in the strategies — they are in a shared helper, so the strategies are one-line wrappers. The abstraction carries no information.
The shared helper is a hidden dependency every strategy needs, so they are not independently testable.
4 files × 5 lines plus a factory plus a helper: more code, same coupling.
The fix

Decide honestly: either (a) the branches are trivial → keep the switch and delete the four classes, or (b) the algorithms are genuinely different → move the logic into the strategies and give each one a real test file.

Selection from data: const STRATEGIES: Record<Segment, PricingStrategy> — adding a segment adds a key and a class, and nothing else. In TypeScript, satisfies Record<…> gives compile-time exhaustiveness.
Where a switch genuinely remains (segment selection from a raw string off the wire), keep it in one obvious place and make the default explicit.
If several strategies share 80% of their logic, extract that into a *domain service* they take as a collaborator — not a base class.
Add the metrics (pricing.strategy label) that justify the abstraction.
Ask the team first

practice.title: Scenario 12 — A retry that duplicates charges
items: Difficulty
The design
Defects, worst first
Retrying a non-idempotent write. A timeout does not mean the charge failed; the money may have moved. This is a correctness bug with financial consequences.
No idempotency key. The provider almost certainly supports one; it is not being used.
Fixed-delay retries with no jitter → synchronised retries across instances (a thundering herd during a gateway slowdown).
No retry budget → retries can exceed the caller's deadline and the work is wasted anyway.
Reconciliation is a nightly human process, not an automated repair; a 24-hour exposure window.
No breaker: retries amplify load on an already-struggling gateway.
The fix

Stop retrying immediately. Generate a stable idempotency key per *logical* payment attempt (e.g. orderId:paymentAttempt) and pass it on every retry. A provider that supports idempotency keys makes retries safe.
If the provider has no idempotency support, treat a timeout as unknown, not failed: do not retry; raise a PaymentUnknown state; reconcile via a status query or the gateway's reconciliation API.
Exponential backoff with full jitter and a retry budget nested inside the caller's deadline.
Add a circuit breaker so the whole payment path sheds load instead of amplifying it.
Replace the nightly report with an automated reconciliation loop (poll unknown charges to resolution, escalate only true exceptions) and alert on age.
Model the payment as a state machine (initiated → authorized → captured → failed | unknown | reversed) so every state is explicit and every transition is idempotent.
Ask the team first

Plan the exit: decide the threshold (services, teams, compliance need) under which you remove it, and write it down.
Ask the team first

practice.title: Scenario 10 — Serverless with a connection pool per invocation
items: Difficulty
The design
Defects, worst first
Connection storm: 1,000 concurrent invocations × 10 connections = 10,000 connections against a limit of ~200. The database is the outage cause.
No timeouts on downstream calls → cold starts plus unbounded latency; no init-duration visibility.
Batch failures are all-or-nothing: one poison message fails the batch and 9 good messages are retried forever.
Retries without a DLQ and without idempotency → duplicate processing, unbounded cost.
No concurrency cap, so a queue burst instantiates unbounded handlers and amplifies the DB problem.
Cold start is blamed, but the real cost is connection initialisation per invocation.
The fix
Module-scope pool (reused per warm container) sized to db_max_connections × share; or RDS Proxy/PgBouncer; or front the function with a queue with bounded concurrency.
Batched DB access; a single query or a batch API instead of per-row queries.
Handle each record in a batch independently and return batchItemFailures; DLQ the poison message with the payload and error.
Reserved concurrency per function to protect downstream dependencies; a per-user rate limit if fan-out is unbounded.
Explicit timeout on every downstream call; instrument Init Duration separately from handler duration.
Move long-running work out of the function; use a worker for anything beyond the timeout.
Thin handler + reusable core module (the B pattern from 11.3.9).
Ask the team first

practice.title: Scenario 11 — A Strategy that is a switch in disguise
items: Difficulty
The design
Defects, worst first
The decision is still in one place and is still closed to extension. Adding a segment edits the factory. This is the *entire* cost of Strategy with none of the benefit.
The algorithms are not in the strategies — they are in a shared helper, so the strategies are one-line wrappers. The abstraction carries no information.
The shared helper is a hidden dependency every strategy needs, so they are not independently testable.
4 files × 5 lines plus a factory plus a helper: more code, same coupling.
The fix

Decide honestly: either (a) the branches are trivial → keep the switch and delete the four classes, or (b) the algorithms are genuinely different → move the logic into the strategies and give each one a real test file.

Selection from data: const STRATEGIES: Record<Segment, PricingStrategy> — adding a segment adds a key and a class, and nothing else. In TypeScript, satisfies Record<…> gives compile-time exhaustiveness.
Where a switch genuinely remains (segment selection from a raw string off the wire), keep it in one obvious place and make the default explicit.
If several strategies share 80% of their logic, extract that into a *domain service* they take as a collaborator — not a base class.
Add the metrics (pricing.strategy label) that justify the abstraction.
Ask the team first

practice.title: Scenario 12 — A retry that duplicates charges
items: Difficulty
The design
Defects, worst first
Retrying a non-idempotent write. A timeout does not mean the charge failed; the money may have moved. This is a correctness bug with financial consequences.
No idempotency key. The provider almost certainly supports one; it is not being used.
Fixed-delay retries with no jitter → synchronised retries across instances (a thundering herd during a gateway slowdown).
No retry budget → retries can exceed the caller's deadline and the work is wasted anyway.
Reconciliation is a nightly human process, not an automated repair; a 24-hour exposure window.
No breaker: retries amplify load on an already-struggling gateway.
The fix

Stop retrying immediately. Generate a stable idempotency key per *logical* payment attempt (e.g. orderId:paymentAttempt) and pass it on every retry. A provider that supports idempotency keys makes retries safe.
If the provider has no idempotency support, treat a timeout as unknown, not failed: do not retry; raise a PaymentUnknown state; reconcile via a status query or the gateway's reconciliation API.
Exponential backoff with full jitter and a retry budget nested inside the caller's deadline.
Add a circuit breaker so the whole payment path sheds load instead of amplifying it.
Replace the nightly report with an automated reconciliation loop (poll unknown charges to resolution, escalate only true exceptions) and alert on age.
Model the payment as a state machine (initiated → authorized → captured → failed | unknown | reversed) so every state is explicit and every transition is idempotent.
Ask the team first

topics.title: Singleton
topics.description: Singleton restricts a class to exactly one instance and provides a global point of access to it.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Why it is almost always the wrong answer

It is a hidden dependency. AppConfig.getInstance() appears in the middle of a function whose signature promises nothing about configuration. The dependency is invisible to the reader, to the type system, and to every tool that traces calls. Compare new BillingService(config) — the dependency is in the signature, greppable, and free to vary.

It is untestable. You cannot pass a different instance to the code under test. Tests mutate global state, so they cannot run in parallel and they leak state between cases. This is why singleton code produces the notorious beforeEach { Config.reset() } in every spec file that touches it.

It owns its own lifecycle. Singletons initialise lazily, forever, on first use. In a server, that means initialisation can happen on the hot path of the first request under a lock; in a test, it means state survives between tests. Both are the container's job, not the class's.

It destroys testability of module boundaries. It creates a *global mutable variable*, which means any two parts of the program can interfere. Under concurrency you now need to reason about which of your 40 threads might be reading config mid-reassignment.

It is not actually one instance, it is one instance per realm. In Node with ESM/CJS interop you get two; in a browser with iframes you get several; in a cluster you get one *per worker*. So Singleton usually fails to deliver even the thing it promises while still delivering the costs.
Real code: the three replacements, in order of preference
A genuinely defensible Singleton
The object is stateless or immutable (a pure function table, a lookup table of currency codes, a regex cache). Then "singleton" degenerates to "module constant" and there is no coupling problem.

The object is a process-level resource with expensive acquisition — a thread pool, a native library handle, an open TLS context. Here the real concerns are thread-safe lazy init and guaranteed release. Prefer an explicit acquire()/release() or a container-managed singleton over a class-managed one.
The language/runtime gives you process-wide state anyway — a global event loop, a standard output stream, an interpreter registry — and re-implementing it adds nothing.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain difficulty and when you would use it.
Explain why it is almost always the wrong answer and when you would use it.
Explain a genuinely defensible singleton and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Singleton gives you: cheap access, one guaranteed instance, a natural home for process-wide caches. It costs you: invisible coupling, impossible isolation, poor concurrency semantics, lifecycle you cannot control, and — the one that bites hardest — a codebase where *every* class could secretly reach *every* other class, so the dependency graph is a star with the Singleton at the centre and no edges you can see.

topics.title: Factory
topics.description: Factory within Design Patterns.
keyConcepts: Difficulty

Factory Method defines an interface for *creating one kind of object* (a single product) and defers the concrete class to subclasses. The method that builds the thing lives in the same class hierarchy as the thing being built, or in a dedicated creator that subclasses override.

Abstract Factory provides an interface for creating a *family of related objects* without specifying their concrete classes. The caller gets a "kit" whose parts are guaranteed to be mutually compatible.
The concrete vs abstract distinction you must be able to state
When abstract factory is the right answer (and it is a narrow answer)
Factory Method has one abstract creation method per creator class.
Abstract Factory has several abstract creation methods per factory, and returns products of *several* types.
Abstract Factory is usually composed *with* a strategy or registry to select the family.
Real code: the version you will actually write in a service
Factory Method: when a base class owns an algorithm with one variable step and you want subclasses to vary only that step. Also when you need to *test* the algorithm with a stub product.
Abstract Factory: when product families must be mutually consistent and the number of families is small.
Not: when you have one product and no anticipated variation — new PostgresUserRepo(db) is better than RepoFactory.create('postgres', db).

tradeoffs: Both add a layer and a place for the bug to hide (UnknownChannelError at 3am is not fun). Both make stack traces longer and make "find all places that construct X" a semantic search instead of a grep. What they buy: the caller stops depending on concrete classes, which is what makes the system testable and swappable. What they cost: you cannot grep your way to all construction sites any more, so you need the factory to be the one obvious place — otherwise you will end up with four half-implemented factories and a "why does the test env use a different DB driver" bug.

topics.title: Middleware
topics.description: middleware.ts (or src/middleware.ts) runs before a matched request is handled — before pages, route handlers, and rewrites — on the Edge runtime by default.
keyConcepts: Ordering
What middleware can and cannot do
Auth in middleware: the pattern and its limits
The classic redirect loop
Broad matcher including /login. Fix: exclude auth routes explicitly (matcher regex or next.config).

Cookie present but invalid. Middleware checks presence only; the page's requireUser() sees an invalid session and redirects to /login; middleware sees the cookie still present and redirects to /dashboard; infinite loop. Fix: middleware must delete the cookie when it rejects, and the deep check must cookies().delete() on failure.

Param-aware routes. Middleware uses pathname only, so /login?next=/login or an i18n prefix mismatch loops. Fix: normalize with the same prefixes your routes use and validate next to prevent open redirects.
Trailing slash / case mismatch producing /Login which doesn't match your exclusion.
Rewrite loops: rewriting to a path that matches your own matcher again.
commonMistakes: doing DB authorization in Edge middleware; mutating req.nextUrl in place instead of cloning; matching everything and slowing every request; treating middleware as the only auth check; forgetting that middleware can run on RSC/prefetch requests and must be cheap; using redirect() in middleware when you meant an internal rewrite.
practiceTasks: implement middleware with a narrow matcher, a presence-only session gate, a safe next redirect parameter (validate it is a same-origin relative path), and a debug header x-mw: allowed|redirected. Then deliberately create each of the five loop causes above, observe the redirect chain with curl -I -L, and fix each by editing only middleware or requireUser(). Add a test asserting exactly one redirect for an invalid cookie.

interviewQuestions.text: When does middleware run in the request lifecycle?
What does the `config.matcher` do and why prefer it over pathname checks?
Can middleware do authorization? Why not?
What is the redirect loop bug and what causes it?
interviewQuestions.answer: *Context.* A /dashboard route 307s to /login and the browser reports "too many redirects". *Decision.* Trace the two redirect sources as separate actors: the middleware gate and the data-layer session check, and find out which pair is disagreeing. *Reasoning.* The canonical cause is a split-brain: middleware validates *presence* of the session cookie while the page calls requireUser(), which validates the session *value*. When the session is expired, revoked, or signed with a rotated key, the cookie still exists. Middleware therefore admits the request, requireUser() rejects it and redirects to /login, middleware sees the cookie still present and redirects back to /dashboard. Neither component is wrong in isolation; the missing invariant is that the cookie's presence must imply its validity, or that rejection must clear the cookie. *Trade-offs.* Full verification in middleware (JWT signature check, session lookup) is cheap for stateless JWTs and expensive for database sessions on the Edge; verifying fully makes every request pay that cost and still leaves object-level authorization undone. *Failure scenario.* A key rotation invalidates all sessions; 100% of authenticated traffic 307-loops, error monitors fill with 3xx chains, and login itself appears broken. *Prevention.* Clear the cookie on rejection at every layer; make the matcher exclude /login and static assets; keep one requireUser() used by pages, handlers, and actions; add a synthetic check that requests a protected route with an invalid session cookie and asserts a single redirect to /login, plus a loop detector alert on repeated redirect chains.

topics.title: Dependency injection
topics.description: Dependency Injection (DI) is supplying a class's collaborators from outside rather than constructing them inside. Inversion of Control (IoC) is the general principle; a container is one mechanism for achieving it. Critical distinction: DI does not require a container.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Why DI
Fakes instead of mocks. A constructor parameter typed as an interface can be replaced with an in-memory implementation. A new inside a method cannot.

Determinism. Inject Clock, IdGenerator, Random, and your tests stop being flaky. A codebase that injects Clock has no jest.useFakeTimers; a codebase that calls Date.now() deep in a domain service has flaky tests forever.
Scope control. Whether something is a singleton, per-request, or per-test becomes a decision in the composition root rather than an accident of static.
Decoupling for change. Swapping a payment provider touches the composition root and the adapter, not the service.
The five kinds of injection, and which to use
An IoC container
Registration: bind(Foo).to(PostgresFoo), bind(Token).to(Impl).singleton(), bind(Foo).toFactory(...).
Resolution: the container walks the graph, resolving each constructor parameter by type token, recursively. This is why it must handle circular dependencies — and why it usually cannot.
Lifetimes: transient (new each time), singleton (one per container), scoped (one per request — the one you usually want), container (one per DI container in a modular system).
Wiring by type token: interfaces need a token (the interface type itself, or a symbol/string) since you cannot new an interface.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain difficulty and when you would use it.
Explain the five kinds of injection, and which to use and when you would use it.
Explain an ioc container and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: *Gain:* you stop repeating new chains, you get lifetimes and scoping for free, you can swap bindings per environment. *Cost:* your dependency graph becomes runtime data. Debuggers cannot follow it, stack traces get a resolution frame, mistakes become startup-time "no registration for X" instead of compile-time errors, IDE "go to definition" breaks, and the graph can hide coupling that looks clean in the code. The worst outcome is a codebase where classes have no constructors at all and take everything from a service locator — that is DI without any of its benefits: still hidden dependencies, but now untyped.

topics.title: Builder
topics.description: Builder constructs a complex object by accumulating configuration in steps, then calling build(). It solves the *telescoping constructor*: a class whose constructor signature grows one parameter per optional feature, producing call sites like new HttpClient(a, b, undefined, c, undefined, d, false).
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The problem, stated precisely
Builder with mandatory fields done properly
Immutable-with-copy builder

Use: ≥4 optional configuration axes; options that must be mutually exclusive or require cross-field validation; objects whose construction involves intermediate expensive steps (buffers, streams, compiled SQL); fixtures in tests (a userBuilder() that gives you valid defaults and one override per call is one of the highest-value builders in any codebase).
Don't use: when the object has 2–3 simple fields — a builder is more code than the constructor and nobody asked for it.
Don't use: to hide a missing required field instead of modelling it — a builder that lets you build an invalid object is worse than a constructor.
Don't use as a general substitute for "just pass the dependencies" — DI does that job better.
Build once, cache the built object. A builder that creates a new connection pool per call is a bug factory. Builders are for *configuration*, not per-request work.
Builder validation errors must be aggregate, not fail-fast on the first field. A user-facing builder that reports one error per round trip is a bad experience.
If a builder is used to build an untrusted object (from JSON), you must validate the values, not just the presence of fields; the type system is not involved at that boundary.
Builders that set security-relevant fields (auth headers, TLS verification) should not be publicly reachable from request input. Make the sensitive setters internal or require a token object.

Benefit: call sites become self-documenting, validation has a whole-object view, and the "optional with a default" explosion stops. Note that the copy-builder (withX) removes the mutable-window problem and is often strictly better than the classic builder in TypeScript — say that in the interview, it is a distinguishing point.

topics.title: Facade
topics.description: Facade within Design Patterns.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Adapter
Facade
Bridge
Interviewer recognition test

Adapter: always, whenever a third-party or legacy interface meets your interface. Cost is near zero and the payoff (one place to fix vendor breakage) is enormous. This is the highest value-to-cost ratio pattern in the entire catalog.
Facade: when a caller needs a *workflow*, not a single operation. Do not use it to hide a single subsystem's API — a facade with one subsystem is a pointless wrapper.
Bridge: when you can name two axes that both change. If you can only name one, you want a plain interface. Bridge is the most frequently over-applied of the three.

Adapter adds a call frame and hides the vendor's real capabilities — a developer debugging a Stripe error has to know an adapter exists, which means the adapter needs good error wrapping (StripeAdapterError with vendorCode preserved). Never swallow the vendor error into new Error('Payment failed').

Facade hides capability, which is great for consumers and terrible for the platform team. It also becomes an attractive nuisance: everyone adds a method to it, and it turns into a God object with 90 methods. Mitigate by having several narrow facades (CheckoutFacade, AdminFacade) rather than one PlatformFacade.
Bridge doubles the number of classes before it produces any value, and makes the stack traces longer.

Adapters are where vendor API version drift lives. Pin the vendor SDK version, and write a contract test suite that runs against the vendor's sandbox in CI so a breaking change fails the build rather than production.

topics.title: Proxy
topics.description: A Proxy is a stand-in for another object that intercepts operations on it. In design-pattern terms it is the structural version of Decorator: instead of hand-forwarding each method, you intercept property access generically. JavaScript ships this as a language feature, so "the Proxy pattern" and "the JS Proxy API" are the same conversation.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Real uses, in rough order of production value
Boundary validation and normalisation. A Proxy in front of parsed external input converts "trust the payload" into "validate the payload", without you writing a DTO per field.
Lazy initialisation / virtual fields. A Proxy that materialises a field from a loader on first access removes the if (!this.x) this.x = load() pattern from constructors.

Memoisation. Intercept get, look up a WeakMap cache, compute on miss. Careful: the cache key must be the *receiver*, not the proxy, or you get infinite recursion. And you must not memoise anything with a side effect.
Read-only views. A Proxy that throws on set/delete/defineProperty makes immutability real rather than readonly-by-convention (readonly in TypeScript compiles away; Object.freeze is shallow).
Deprecation shims and API migration. Wrap a legacy module and log which old methods are still called — you get migration telemetry for free, and the shim disappears when the log goes quiet.
ORM/SDK property-access translation — a snake_case API exposed as camelCase.
Tracing instrumentation — the logged decorator from 11.1.6.
Use when the interception is *generic* (applies to all properties) or *derived from data* (a spec-driven validator), or when the value is genuinely lazy and expensive.
Use in dev/test code: a debug Proxy that logs unexpected property reads is a fantastic way to find which properties of a mock a test actually depends on.
Don't use on hot paths: every property access becomes a trap with megamorphic dispatch; a Proxy-heavy inner loop can be several times slower than the plain version, and it defeats inline caches.

tradeoffs: You gain: one place for a whole class of concerns, zero per-field code, composability. You pay: (a) readability — a reader sees p.foo and cannot know a trap runs; (b) debuggability — the stack shows the proxy, not the target; (c) invariants — you can throw TypeError from a proxy that violates an invariant, which is the worst class of bug; (d) performance on hot paths; (e) typeof, instanceof, and identity subtleties that surprise people (p instanceof Foo works; p.constructor returns your trapped value if you trap it wrong).

topics.title: Anti-patterns
topics.description: A pattern anti-pattern is the application of a named pattern in a context where its costs exceed its benefits — producing code that is more abstract, less readable, and no more correct than what it replaced.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Has the variability actually arrived? Not "might". Has it arrived twice already?
Is the number of participants small enough that a reader can hold it? More than ~5 participants in a diagram and you have lost more than you gained.
Is the pattern's cost concentrated where it hurts most? Indirection in a hot loop or in a CRUD endpoint hurts; indirection in a rarely-changed extension point does not.
Anti-pattern catalogue, one per pattern, with the smell and the fix
The two most important anti-patterns in practice

The Pattern Tax. When a team learns patterns, they start converting *every* if into a class. The measurable outcome: 400 files instead of 60, a new hire takes 3 weeks to understand the checkout flow, and the "flexibility" is never used. The fix is a written rule: *a new file requires a named axis of variation.* Reviewers enforce it. This single rule prevents more damage than any pattern advice.

Diagrammatic Design. Choosing a pattern because the UML diagram looks impressive, not because a stated requirement varies. The tell: nobody can name the requirement that would justify the indirection. The fix in an interview is to be asked "which requirement drove this?" — if you cannot answer, revert.
How to review someone else's patterns
Point to the requirement that makes this abstract. If there is none, it should be concrete.
Count the participants. Over ~5 in one collaboration, the reader's working memory is now the bottleneck.
Find the decision. Where does the choice of implementation live? If it is a switch, the abstraction is decorative.
commonMistakes: Treating "pattern anti-pattern" as licence to write unstructured code.
Removing a pattern from a codebase that genuinely varies, to look minimal.
Reviewing patterns by name rather than by requirement.

topics.title: What a pattern is, and the three things every pattern has
topics.description: A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem. It is not a library, not a language feature, and — critically — not code you copy. It is *vocabulary plus structure plus a documented cost*. When a reviewer says "that's a Strategy here," they are not commenting on your code style; they are naming a known trade-off so the next person does not have to rediscover it.
keyConcepts: Difficulty

Intent — what problem it solves, stated in one sentence that does not mention the solution's mechanics. "Allow a client to add new behaviour without changing a class that already uses it." Note the absence of the word "Strategy." A pattern's intent should survive a total rewrite of its implementation.

Participants — the collaborating classes with the roles they play and, crucially, *which roles are optional*. A pattern's participants include things that are frequently forgotten ("the Subject must also provide attach/detach") and things that are frequently mistaken for requirements ("the ConcreteObserver does not need to know about the Subject").

Consequences — what you gain, what you pay, and the questions the pattern defers. Consequences are the whole point. A pattern whose consequences section says "none, it's just better" is marketing, not engineering.
The forcing function. What makes the naive version hurt. (Six subclasses and every new country is a new class? Fifteen constructor arguments and call sites are unreadable?)
The structure. The participants and who holds references to whom.
The mechanics. What actually happens at runtime, message by message.
The bill. Consequences: what it costs, what new problems it creates, when to undo it.
The four-part vocabulary you should be able to recite
The three levels of pattern, and why the distinction matters
Idioms — low-level, language-specific, invisible in the diagram. const over let, a guard clause, early return, a named boolean. Idioms are what a reviewer comments on in a line-level review.
Design patterns — object-level structure. Singleton, Strategy, Observer, Command. These show up in class diagrams and are the subject of 11.1.

interviewQuestions.text: Why does this pattern exist?
interviewQuestions.answer: Ensure a class has exactly one instance and provide a global access point.

interviewQuestions.text: What concrete problem in the naive code forces its use?
interviewQuestions.answer: Two AppConfig objects with divergent values; tests that cannot stub the config.

interviewQuestions.text: Who knows about whom?
interviewQuestions.answer: Client → Singleton; Singleton holds private static instance; no one holds a reference to anyone.

interviewQuestions.text: What did I just buy and what did I just pay?
interviewQuestions.answer: Shared state by construction; harder to test; hidden dependency; lifecycle owned by the class, not the container.

tradeoffs: Every pattern has (a) an indirection cost at runtime or in reading, (b) a mental cost for the next reader, (c) a *localisation* cost — the logic that used to be in one readable block is now spread across files. The only reason to pay (a)+(b)+(c) is that the thing being abstracted changes faster than the reader can re-learn it.

topics.title: Singleton and why it is almost always the wrong answer
topics.description: Singleton restricts a class to exactly one instance and provides a global point of access to it.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Why it is almost always the wrong answer

It is a hidden dependency. AppConfig.getInstance() appears in the middle of a function whose signature promises nothing about configuration. The dependency is invisible to the reader, to the type system, and to every tool that traces calls. Compare new BillingService(config) — the dependency is in the signature, greppable, and free to vary.

It is untestable. You cannot pass a different instance to the code under test. Tests mutate global state, so they cannot run in parallel and they leak state between cases. This is why singleton code produces the notorious beforeEach { Config.reset() } in every spec file that touches it.

It owns its own lifecycle. Singletons initialise lazily, forever, on first use. In a server, that means initialisation can happen on the hot path of the first request under a lock; in a test, it means state survives between tests. Both are the container's job, not the class's.

It destroys testability of module boundaries. It creates a *global mutable variable*, which means any two parts of the program can interfere. Under concurrency you now need to reason about which of your 40 threads might be reading config mid-reassignment.

It is not actually one instance, it is one instance per realm. In Node with ESM/CJS interop you get two; in a browser with iframes you get several; in a cluster you get one *per worker*. So Singleton usually fails to deliver even the thing it promises while still delivering the costs.
Real code: the three replacements, in order of preference
A genuinely defensible Singleton
The object is stateless or immutable (a pure function table, a lookup table of currency codes, a regex cache). Then "singleton" degenerates to "module constant" and there is no coupling problem.

The object is a process-level resource with expensive acquisition — a thread pool, a native library handle, an open TLS context. Here the real concerns are thread-safe lazy init and guaranteed release. Prefer an explicit acquire()/release() or a container-managed singleton over a class-managed one.
The language/runtime gives you process-wide state anyway — a global event loop, a standard output stream, an interpreter registry — and re-implementing it adds nothing.

tradeoffs: Singleton gives you: cheap access, one guaranteed instance, a natural home for process-wide caches. It costs you: invisible coupling, impossible isolation, poor concurrency semantics, lifecycle you cannot control, and — the one that bites hardest — a codebase where *every* class could secretly reach *every* other class, so the dependency graph is a star with the Singleton at the centre and no edges you can see.

topics.title: Factory Method, Abstract Factory, and the concrete vs abstract distinction
topics.description: Factory Method, Abstract Factory, and the concrete vs abstract distinction within Design Patterns.
keyConcepts: Difficulty

Factory Method defines an interface for *creating one kind of object* (a single product) and defers the concrete class to subclasses. The method that builds the thing lives in the same class hierarchy as the thing being built, or in a dedicated creator that subclasses override.

Abstract Factory provides an interface for creating a *family of related objects* without specifying their concrete classes. The caller gets a "kit" whose parts are guaranteed to be mutually compatible.
The concrete vs abstract distinction you must be able to state
When abstract factory is the right answer (and it is a narrow answer)
Factory Method has one abstract creation method per creator class.
Abstract Factory has several abstract creation methods per factory, and returns products of *several* types.
Abstract Factory is usually composed *with* a strategy or registry to select the family.
Real code: the version you will actually write in a service
Factory Method: when a base class owns an algorithm with one variable step and you want subclasses to vary only that step. Also when you need to *test* the algorithm with a stub product.
Abstract Factory: when product families must be mutually consistent and the number of families is small.
Not: when you have one product and no anticipated variation — new PostgresUserRepo(db) is better than RepoFactory.create('postgres', db).

tradeoffs: Both add a layer and a place for the bug to hide (UnknownChannelError at 3am is not fun). Both make stack traces longer and make "find all places that construct X" a semantic search instead of a grep. What they buy: the caller stops depending on concrete classes, which is what makes the system testable and swappable. What they cost: you cannot grep your way to all construction sites any more, so you need the factory to be the one obvious place — otherwise you will end up with four half-implemented factories and a "why does the test env use a different DB driver" bug.

topics.title: Builder and the telescoping-constructor problem it solves
topics.description: Builder constructs a complex object by accumulating configuration in steps, then calling build(). It solves the *telescoping constructor*: a class whose constructor signature grows one parameter per optional feature, producing call sites like new HttpClient(a, b, undefined, c, undefined, d, false).
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The problem, stated precisely
Builder with mandatory fields done properly
Immutable-with-copy builder

Use: ≥4 optional configuration axes; options that must be mutually exclusive or require cross-field validation; objects whose construction involves intermediate expensive steps (buffers, streams, compiled SQL); fixtures in tests (a userBuilder() that gives you valid defaults and one override per call is one of the highest-value builders in any codebase).
Don't use: when the object has 2–3 simple fields — a builder is more code than the constructor and nobody asked for it.
Don't use: to hide a missing required field instead of modelling it — a builder that lets you build an invalid object is worse than a constructor.
Don't use as a general substitute for "just pass the dependencies" — DI does that job better.
Build once, cache the built object. A builder that creates a new connection pool per call is a bug factory. Builders are for *configuration*, not per-request work.
Builder validation errors must be aggregate, not fail-fast on the first field. A user-facing builder that reports one error per round trip is a bad experience.
If a builder is used to build an untrusted object (from JSON), you must validate the values, not just the presence of fields; the type system is not involved at that boundary.
Builders that set security-relevant fields (auth headers, TLS verification) should not be publicly reachable from request input. Make the sensitive setters internal or require a token object.

tradeoffs: Cost: one more class per complex type, an extra allocation, a mutable window in the classic form, and a longer type signature chain that some IDEs handle poorly. Benefit: call sites become self-documenting, validation has a whole-object view, and the "optional with a default" explosion stops. Note that the copy-builder (withX) removes the mutable-window problem and is often strictly better than the classic builder in TypeScript — say that in the interview, it is a distinguishing point.

topics.title: Adapter, Facade, and Bridge
topics.description: Adapter, Facade, and Bridge within Design Patterns.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Adapter
Facade
Bridge
Interviewer recognition test

Adapter: always, whenever a third-party or legacy interface meets your interface. Cost is near zero and the payoff (one place to fix vendor breakage) is enormous. This is the highest value-to-cost ratio pattern in the entire catalog.
Facade: when a caller needs a *workflow*, not a single operation. Do not use it to hide a single subsystem's API — a facade with one subsystem is a pointless wrapper.
Bridge: when you can name two axes that both change. If you can only name one, you want a plain interface. Bridge is the most frequently over-applied of the three.

Adapter adds a call frame and hides the vendor's real capabilities — a developer debugging a Stripe error has to know an adapter exists, which means the adapter needs good error wrapping (StripeAdapterError with vendorCode preserved). Never swallow the vendor error into new Error('Payment failed').

Facade hides capability, which is great for consumers and terrible for the platform team. It also becomes an attractive nuisance: everyone adds a method to it, and it turns into a God object with 90 methods. Mitigate by having several narrow facades (CheckoutFacade, AdminFacade) rather than one PlatformFacade.
Bridge doubles the number of classes before it produces any value, and makes the stack traces longer.

Adapters are where vendor API version drift lives. Pin the vendor SDK version, and write a contract test suite that runs against the vendor's sandbox in CI so a breaking change fails the build rather than production.

topics.title: Decorator vs Wrapper, and where JavaScript's own language features do this for free
topics.description: A Decorator attaches additional behaviour to an object by *wrapping it* while keeping the same interface. A "wrapper" in the looser sense is anything that holds a target and forwards to it; the difference is that a Decorator is expected to preserve the interface exactly, so it is substitutable for the thing it wraps.
keyConcepts: Difficulty

Not all methods are forwarded. If Notifier grows sendBatch next month and the decorator forwards only send, the decorator silently stops being substitutable. Prefer an explicit implements and let the compiler catch it — or a Proxy-based generic decorator for interface-agnostic wrapping.
Decorating the *identity*. Code that does if (a === b) or uses the object as a Map key breaks if the decorator returns a different object. Pass identity through explicitly when it matters.

Changing the return type. RetryingNotifier returning Promise<void> where the inner returns a receipt means the interface is not preserved and callers lose information. Decide whether decorators can narrow/transform values; if yes, document it.
Where the language does this for free
Proxy and Reflect — the built-in decorator. Use it for tracing, validation at the boundary, memoisation, and lazy loading; do not use it on the hot data path because every access becomes a trap.
Default parameters and ?? — optional configuration. function f(a, { retries = 3, timeout = 5000 } = {}) is a Builder for two fields. Do not build a class.

Middlewares as a chain — an array of (next) => (input) => output functions is the decorator pattern with less ceremony, and it composes left-to-right by array order. Express/Koa/Redux middleware chains are Decorator; when you say "we use decorators for cross-cutting concerns", a reviewer may ask why you did not just add one middleware.

Use: cross-cutting concerns that apply to a *subset* of instances or calls, at runtime-determined combinations, where inheritance would multiply. Canonical: logging, timing, retries, caching, authorisation, transaction boundaries, idempotency keys, circuit breaking.
Use when you need the decoration to be data-driven — a list of concerns chosen per-tenant or per-endpoint. That is the real reason decorators exist that Template Method does not cover.

Don't use: for concerns that apply to *all* instances (put them in the class or in a framework-level middleware), or when there is only one combination (no composition is happening, so you have added a layer for nothing).
Don't use: as an excuse to avoid naming a concept. If "Retry" is a decorator around send, then RetryPolicy is a decorator around send too — you have two names for one thing.

tradeoffs: Cost: an extra object and a call frame per layer; stack traces get long and uninformative (at Decorator.send … at Decorator.send …); debugging requires unwinding; the wrapper must be kept in sync with the interface by hand (the single biggest source of bugs). Benefit: no combinatorial class explosion, runtime-selectable composition, per-instance configuration, and clean ordering semantics.

topics.title: Observer and the event emitter as its canonical implementation
topics.description: Observer defines a one-to-many dependency: when a Subject changes state, all registered Observers are notified automatically. The canonical implementation in every language is the event emitter / event bus.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
on returns an unsubscribe function. If it does not, you cannot remove a listener, and you leak the listener *and its captured scope* for the life of the process.

A Set, not an array. Duplicate subscriptions are a real bug class (a module re-imported in dev adds the listener twice; you get double-sent notifications in dev only, which is the worst possible place to find it).

Copy before iterating. A listener that unsubscribes during dispatch otherwise mutates the collection mid-loop: in JS that skips listeners; in other languages it throws ConcurrentModificationException. This is a genuine production incident (self-unsubscribing one-shot listeners).
Per-event keying. A single array means off is O(n) and emit must filter; a Map<event, Set> makes both cheap and makes "no listeners for this event" detectable.

Typed event map. Record<string, unknown> gives you a compile error when a payload shape changes and a typo error on the event name. This is the difference between an event bus as an asset and as a liability.

Error isolation. The version above lets a throwing listener abort the remaining listeners. That is a decision: decide it explicitly. The robust version catches per-listener, reports the error, and continues — because "one bad analytics listener stopped order confirmation" is a real bug.
Observer's two cousins and the distinction that matters
Observer: the Subject *knows* its Observers and typically calls them directly. Coupling is compile-time visible.

Reactive (RxJS): cold/hot semantics, backpressure via bufferSize, cancellation via AbortSignal, and switchMap/concatMap for concurrency control. If you have any rate-limited source, you want this, not a callback list.
Pub/Sub (11.1.17): publishers and subscribers never reference each other, usually across a broker.

Use: when the set of reactions to an event is *open* (will grow), when reactions are optional and independent (analytics, cache invalidation, email), when the number of subscribers varies per deployment, or when you genuinely want to break a compile-time dependency on a downstream consumer.

topics.title: Command and the undo stack
topics.description: Command encapsulates a request as an object. That object can carry parameters, be stored, be queued, be logged, and — the reason the pattern exists in most UI code — be *executed later or reversed*.
keyConcepts: Difficulty

Non-invertible commands. ResizeCanvas(w, h) cannot be inverted without storing the old size. So every invertible command must capture its prior state *at construction or execute time*, not try to reconstruct it at undo time.

Partial failure. MoveShape succeeded, RecolorShape failed. Now the stack top is RecolorShape, which never ran, but the state reflects a moved shape. You must decide: push only on success (above), or push before and mark as failed. The correct default is push only on success and record the failure separately.

Non-LIFO dependencies. Undoing AddB after AddA was undone breaks the invariant. This is why real editors store *commands in a document timeline* with an inverse stored at execution time, not a naive stack.

Server authority. Undo on the client that the server disagrees with is a data-integrity incident. Undo must be a *command sent to the authority* that returns an inverse, not a client-side state edit. This is the difference between undo in Figma and undo in a notepad.

Use: undo/redo; operation queues and job dispatch; operation logging and replay; throttled/serialised access to a mutable resource (each command captures its own parameters so no shared mutable state leaks); anything where you need to *defer* or *retry with identical parameters*.
Use for Command + Invoker + Receiver when you need a queue that serialises access — one worker, commands in order, no locking.
Don't use: for every method call. Wrapping add(a,b) in a AddCommand class with an execute() that calls calculator.add(a,b) adds a class and zero capability.
Don't use when the receiver must run immediately and return a value to the caller — that is a function.
Bounded stack. Never unbounded; a text editor holding a million commands is an OOM. Bound it and make the eviction policy visible ("earliest 100 commands are not undoable").
Redo stack is the mirror: on undo, push the command and any captured inverse onto the redo stack; on execute, clear the redo stack.
Coalescing. Repeated identical commands (typing) should collapse — replace the top of the stack if it has the same coalesceKey and is recent. This is what keeps memory bounded in real editors.

tradeoffs: Gain: deferred/queued execution, serialisability, undo, logging, uniform error handling and retry at the invoker level, and a uniform place to add authorisation/validation ("every command passes through the same guard").

topics.title: Strategy and the switch statement it replaces
topics.description: Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms, encapsulates each in its own class, and makes them independently swappable via a common interface.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The problem
AFTER

Use: when a decision is *made at runtime from data* (config, DB column, request field, user segment), when the alternatives are genuinely different *algorithms* rather than variations of one, and when each alternative has enough behaviour to deserve its own test file.
Use: when you want the *decision to be testable in isolation* — the biggest practical win.
Don't use for a switch over an enum with 3–4 trivial branches, each one line. That is the "switch that is fine"; replacing it with 5 files and a registry is a net loss in readability.
Don't use when all branches share 95% of their body (the Strategy classes become 95% identical, or worse, they all delegate to a shared helper so you gained a layer and no clarity).
Don't use when the alternatives differ only in *data* — that is a table/config, not a strategy. { vip: 0.9, student: 0.85 } beats five classes.
Real code: the dependency-injected version that scales better
Selection must fail loudly. Unknown segment ⇒ explicit default or throw, never undefined.
Strategies hold state? Prefer stateless strategies held in a DI container as singletons; if a strategy must be stateful, construct it per request.
Persistence: the segment string in the database is a contract. Renaming 'vip' to 'vip-annual' without a migration will silently price orders with the default rule. Migrate the data.

tradeoffs: *Gain:* open/closed, runtime swappable, per-strategy tests, no central place where the decision list can rot.

topics.title: State and the state machine connection
topics.description: State lets an object alter its behaviour when its internal state changes, by delegating to a strategy object per state. The object appears unchanged to the client but its *available operations* change.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The problem: the boolean explosion
AFTER
The State-vs-Strategy distinction, precisely (memorise this)
Three concrete benefits you must be able to argue

The legal graph becomes data. You can draw it, put it in a table, generate docs from it, and — critically — write a *reachability test*: enumerate all states and all operations and assert the transition table matches your spec. With a boolean representation this test is impossible to write.
The state name is available for free for metrics, error messages, and API responses. doc.status is this.state.name.
Adding a state does not require auditing every method — you add a class and register it in the transition map.

Use: when an object has (a) ≥3 states, (b) a transition graph with real constraints, (c) behaviour that differs by state, and (d) illegal combinations that must be impossible rather than merely forbidden.
Use for: order/invoice/subscription lifecycles, workflow engines, protocol state machines, game entity AI, UI wizard steps, job pipelines.
Don't use: two states (use a boolean and a guard), or states that differ only in data (use a field).
Don't use: when transitions must be *auditable for compliance* and the transitions happen inside framework callbacks — then persist an explicit transition log/event instead of relying on the object.

tradeoffs: *Gain:* behaviour that cannot be called in the wrong state, self-documenting legal graph, no guard soup, per-state unit tests, free status name.

topics.title: Template Method and the inheritance trap
topics.description: Template Method defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and lets subclasses override specific steps. It is inheritance-based, and that is both its use and its fatal weakness.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The honest case for it
The inheritance trap, stated concretely

The hook explosion. When you need a job that skips validation but adds a transform, you either override validate to return a lie (return ok(rows) without validating), or you get an if in the base class (if (this.shouldValidate)), and now the template has a hole shaped exactly like your new requirement. After three such requirements the template is a switch with steps around it.

Every subclass sees every step. A subclass that only wants to override parsing is forced to implement persist, because the base declared it abstract. You have created coupling to steps it does not care about.

Testing requires subclassing. You cannot test the template without faking the steps, so your test file defines a TestImportJob extends ImportJob — and if the base class has any *concrete* step that touches the network or the DB, your test is broken or slow. Template Method is hostile to composition-based test doubles precisely because the seams are inheritance-based, not constructor-injection-based.
The hierarchy is permanent. Every new variation is a new subclass; the tree only grows. You cannot compose "a CSV fetcher with an S3 parser" because they are peers in the hierarchy, not layers.
Shadowing hazards. A subclass declaring a private method with the same name as a base method silently breaks polymorphism; super.method() calls get confusing.

Use (rarely): algorithm with ≥5 steps and a fixed order, where only 1–2 steps vary, and the number of subclasses will stay under ~3. Classic: JUnit lifecycle hooks, java.util.logging, JDBC Template, ORM lifecycle callbacks, HTTP request pipeline in a framework you control.
Use when you *are building the framework* and want to force an extension structure on your users — the framework author legitimately owns the skeleton.
Don't use in application code you own when there is more than one or two variable steps.
Don't use when you need runtime composition (choose behaviour from data).

tradeoffs: *Gain:* algorithm in one place, guaranteed step order, shared default steps, extension points that are enforced by the compiler.

topics.title: Repository, Unit of Work, and Data Mapper
topics.description: Repository, Unit of Work, and Data Mapper within Design Patterns.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Data Mapper
Repository
Unit of Work
The three tools that replace manual change tracking
Explicit marking (above): registerDirty(obj) — most control, most to forget.
Identity Map + dirty tracking via Object.freeze + a Proxy that records sets (from 11.1.7) — automatic, magic, hard to debug.
Session-attached objects (Hibernate Session, EF DbContext, Active Record) — you give up domain purity and gain automatic change tracking and lazy loading.
The Lazy Loading trap, which is where purity dies
Data Mapper: whenever the storage shape differs from the domain shape, or you want the domain model free of persistence concerns. This is the default choice in a serious codebase.

Repository: when you have multiple aggregates, want to fake them in tests, or want queries expressed in domain language. Do not build a generic BaseRepository<T, TId> that mirrors your ORM — that is a wrapper with no value.
Unit of Work: when a business operation touches several aggregates and must be atomic. If every operation touches exactly one row and the DB's own transaction handles it, a Unit of Work is overhead.

topics.title: Dependency Injection and IoC containers
topics.description: Dependency Injection (DI) is supplying a class's collaborators from outside rather than constructing them inside. Inversion of Control (IoC) is the general principle; a container is one mechanism for achieving it. Critical distinction: DI does not require a container.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Why DI
Fakes instead of mocks. A constructor parameter typed as an interface can be replaced with an in-memory implementation. A new inside a method cannot.

Determinism. Inject Clock, IdGenerator, Random, and your tests stop being flaky. A codebase that injects Clock has no jest.useFakeTimers; a codebase that calls Date.now() deep in a domain service has flaky tests forever.
Scope control. Whether something is a singleton, per-request, or per-test becomes a decision in the composition root rather than an accident of static.
Decoupling for change. Swapping a payment provider touches the composition root and the adapter, not the service.
The five kinds of injection, and which to use
An IoC container
Registration: bind(Foo).to(PostgresFoo), bind(Token).to(Impl).singleton(), bind(Foo).toFactory(...).
Resolution: the container walks the graph, resolving each constructor parameter by type token, recursively. This is why it must handle circular dependencies — and why it usually cannot.
Lifetimes: transient (new each time), singleton (one per container), scoped (one per request — the one you usually want), container (one per DI container in a modular system).
Wiring by type token: interfaces need a token (the interface type itself, or a symbol/string) since you cannot new an interface.

tradeoffs: *Gain:* you stop repeating new chains, you get lifetimes and scoping for free, you can swap bindings per environment. *Cost:* your dependency graph becomes runtime data. Debuggers cannot follow it, stack traces get a resolution frame, mistakes become startup-time "no registration for X" instead of compile-time errors, IDE "go to definition" breaks, and the graph can hide coupling that looks clean in the code. The worst outcome is a codebase where classes have no constructors at all and take everything from a service locator — that is DI without any of its benefits: still hidden dependencies, but now untyped.

topics.title: Circuit breaker, bulkhead, and the resilience pattern family
topics.description: A resilience pattern protects a system from failure in a dependency by failing fast, shedding load, or degrading gracefully, instead of propagating the failure upward.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Circuit breaker
The threshold decision (this is what interviewers ask)
Bulkhead
The rest of the family
Timeout — the single highest-value pattern. Every remote call gets a deadline; the default is "no timeout" which is the worst default.

Retry with exponential backoff + jitter. Jitter is not optional: without it, N clients retry at the same instant after a failure and re-create the overload you were trying to relieve (the *thundering herd*). Use full jitter: sleep = random(0, base * 2^attempt).
Rate limiter (11.4.3) — limit *rate*, breaker limits *failure*.

Fallback / graceful degradation — a cheaper answer when the primary is unavailable (stale cache, default recommendation, "recommendations temporarily unavailable" instead of a 500). Distinguish fallback from circuit-open error: a fallback is a *successful degraded response*.
Load shedding — reject deliberately when overloaded, prioritising important requests. Requires knowing your priority; admission control beats queue collapse.
Hedging — send a duplicate request to a second replica after a delay fraction of the p99; reduces tail latency at the cost of extra load. Use sparingly and only for idempotent reads.
Backpressure — make the queue bounded and reject at the producer. An unbounded queue converts a latency problem into a memory problem and then an outage.

tradeoffs: Every pattern converts *one* failure mode into *another*: latency (queueing), memory (buffering), correctness (stale fallback data), load (retries). The discipline is to have a budget per layer: connect timeout, read timeout, max attempts, total deadline, and make them nested so the inner budget is always smaller than the outer's. A retry budget larger than the caller's deadline is a bug that produces work nobody will read.

topics.title: Saga and the distributed-transaction pattern family
topics.description: A Saga is a sequence of local transactions, each in its own transaction, with compensating actions to undo the logical effects of completed steps when a later step fails. It replaces the 2PC (two-phase commit) database transaction across services.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Why 2PC is not available in microservices
The two flavours, and this is the key question in the interview
Compensation is not rollback. Know these four differences

Compensation cannot undo an observable side effect. email.send() cannot be unsent; you can send an apology. Inventory.decrement() can often be re-incremented but the *history* still shows a decrement, and a warehouse may have physically picked the item. This is the core reason sagas need domain modelling of "semantic rollback".
Compensation may fail, repeatedly. Retry it independently, with its own retry budget, and persist its state so a crash mid-compensation resumes rather than leaks.
Compensation must be idempotent — because it will be retried.

Compensation can be impossible to order. Compensating step 3 without compensating step 2 can leave you worse off (e.g. refunding before cancelling a shipment you then cancel anyway — you end up with a return you did not want). Strict reverse order is the default, and the "already-refunded" checks in compensating actions matter.
Steps: choreography, orchestration, and hybrid
Persistent saga state (this is what makes it production-grade)
Use: when a business transaction spans services and you accept eventual consistency: order + payment + inventory + shipping + notification.
Use: when 2PC is unavailable (different databases, different vendors) or too slow/fragile.

tradeoffs: *Gain:* services stay autonomous and available; no distributed lock; failures are handled explicitly and can be inspected.

topics.title: Pub/Sub, and how it differs from Observer
topics.description: Publish/Subscribe decouples publishers from subscribers *completely*: the publisher does not know subscribers exist, and subscribers do not know publishers exist. Delivery happens through a broker or mediator. Often asynchronous and cross-process.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The precise difference from Observer
The three questions to answer when choosing

Delivery semantics. at-most-once (ack before handling — you lose data on crash), at-least-once (ack after handling — you get duplicates; this is the only sane default), exactly-once (only within a transaction that includes both the inbox write and the effect — i.e. effectively-once, achieved with the inbox table, not by the broker). State clearly: *exactly-once delivery does not exist; effectively-once processing does, via an idempotent inbox in the same local transaction as the effect.*

Ordering. Brokers guarantee order *per partition*, not globally. If OrderPlaced and OrderShipped must be ordered, both must share a partition key (the order id). Cross-entity ordering requires a different design.

Durability and replay. The event log is durable; consumers track their offset. This gives you replay (rebuild read models — 11.3.7), which is the single most valuable property of event-driven systems and should be your main argument for them.

Schema evolution. Producers and consumers deploy independently. Rules: additive changes only; tolerant reader (ignore unknown fields, require the ones you need); never rename or remove a field; new fields must be optional or have defaults; version in the topic name (orders.placed.v2) with a migration period, or a registry with compatibility checks.
Failure semantics. Poison messages (retries exhausted → DLQ), backpressure (consumer lag), poison-pill prevention, and the fact that a slow consumer in a partition blocks that partition.
Events vs commands on a broker

Use for: cross-service notification, scaling consumers independently, building read models, decoupling release cadence, integrating with external parties, decoupling release cadence, telemetry/audit pipelines, workflow fan-out that must not fail the caller.
Use for "domain event inside one service, 2–4 in-process listeners" — here Observer is better (no broker to run, transactions possible, easier debugging).
Don't use for: anything where the caller needs the result; anything where you cannot tolerate eventual consistency; anything where you cannot operate a broker.

tradeoffs: *Gain:* independent deployment and scaling, failure isolation, replay, new consumers with no producer change, natural audit trail.

topics.title: Pattern anti-patterns: when applying a pattern makes it worse
topics.description: A pattern anti-pattern is the application of a named pattern in a context where its costs exceed its benefits — producing code that is more abstract, less readable, and no more correct than what it replaced.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Has the variability actually arrived? Not "might". Has it arrived twice already?
Is the number of participants small enough that a reader can hold it? More than ~5 participants in a diagram and you have lost more than you gained.
Is the pattern's cost concentrated where it hurts most? Indirection in a hot loop or in a CRUD endpoint hurts; indirection in a rarely-changed extension point does not.
Anti-pattern catalogue, one per pattern, with the smell and the fix

The Pattern Tax. When a team learns patterns, they start converting *every* if into a class. Point to the requirement that makes this abstract. If there is none, it should be concrete.
Count the participants. Over ~5 in one collaboration, the reader's working memory is now the bottleneck.
Find the decision. Where does the choice of implementation live? If it is a switch, the abstraction is decorative.
