topics.description: Clean/hexagonal architecture within OOP, SOLID and Clean Code.
keyConcepts: Goroutines are cheap (a few KB of stack, multiplexed onto OS threads by the runtime). Spawning thousands is normal and idiomatic. They have no preemption guarantee in older versions (since Go 1.14, async preemption exists via signals).

Channels are the coordination primitive. Always size the buffer when the producer can outrun the consumer, or the producer blocks; and never close from the send side if senders may still be running. Prefer errgroup for a bounded group of goroutines with automatic error propagation and Wait.

context.Context is the cancellation and deadline mechanism, threaded through every call as the first parameter. It is how you propagate a client disconnect, a request timeout, and a deadline down to the database driver — which is why context.WithTimeout plus defer cancel() on every function that creates one is the single most important Go habit.
errgroup + SetLimit gives you a bulkhead for free:

net/http: the standard library server is production-grade. http.Server has ReadHeaderTimeout (set it or you have a Slowloris vulnerability), ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout, IdleTimeout, and MaxHeaderBytes. Middleware is plain wrapping of http.Handler. Graceful shutdown is srv.Shutdown(ctx) plus closing the listener, waiting for in-flight requests.
Errors are values: no exceptions; wrap with %w for errors.Is/errors.As; a missing error is a programming error. Error strings are lowercase and without punctuation because they compose into messages.
Interfaces are implicit and small: define the interface at the consumer, keep it to one or two methods (io.Reader, error).

Single static binary: cross-compiles with CGO_ENABLED=0 to a few megabytes, no runtime, no dependency manager at deploy time. Containers start in milliseconds and images stay small — an operational advantage that shows up in cold-start scale-out and in distroless/security-scanning terms.

Compile-time safety: static typing with no null, exhaustive-ish error handling, and a language that is small enough to hold in your head. Structs are value types by default; slices and maps are reference types, which is the classic aliasing bug.
Weaknesses to be honest about
Error-handling verbosity: if err != nil everywhere is a real productivity and readability cost; the ecosystem is converging on wrapped errors and helper packages rather than on magic.

Generics are still less pleasant than TypeScript or Java: no higher-kinded types, no Stream-style pipelines, still awkward for higher-order abstractions. Go 1.18+ generics help for containers but have ergonomics complaints (no method constraints on the type-parameter set in some cases).
commonMistakes: not defer cancel()ing contexts; unbounded goroutines without SetLimit; forgetting ReadHeaderTimeout; unbuffered channels between many senders and one receiver; assuming Go's GC solves tail latency by default.
practiceTasks: write a Go service with net/http, errgroup with a concurrency limit of 8, context deadline propagation, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM, and a load test at 20k rps with p99 reported; then repeat in Node and compare.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why is `context.Context` conventionally the first parameter?
🟡 What is the cost of spawning a goroutine compared to a thread?
🟡 Why must channels be buffered when a producer can outrun the consumer?
🔴 What is the loop-variable capture bug in older Go and how does Go 1.22+ change it?
🔴 Explain `errgroup.WithContext` and `SetLimit` and why the limit is a feature.
🔴 Why must you set `ReadHeaderTimeout` on an `http.Server`?
🔴 What's the equivalent of graceful shutdown, and what breaks if you skip it?
🔴 Compare `sync.WaitGroup` and `errgroup` for error propagation.
🔴 When would you choose Go over Node and over Java?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a new internal service that must handle 20k requests per second with p99 under 20ms, where the team has strong Node and Java experience. Decision: I would pick Go for the service and give a short, explicit list of reasons, while naming the real costs. Reasons for Go: goroutines and channels make high IO-bound concurrency simple without an async framework or reactive types; the single static binary means no runtime dependency and fast container starts, which matters for scale-out; context gives first-class cancellation and deadline propagation all the way to the database driver, which is genuinely excellent; and the language surface is small enough that a new engineer is productive in a week. Costs I would state plainly: error handling is more verbose than TypeScript, generics ergonomics are worse, GC tuning for extreme tail latency is less flexible than the JVM's, and the hiring pool is smaller than Java's by a wide margin, so I would only assign people who want to work in Go. Reasoning: the decision hinges on the *shape of the workload*, not on a preference. If this service were mostly blocking JDBC with complex transactional queries, Java with virtual threads would be the better fit; if the team were strongest in Python and this was an ML-adjacent service, Python would win on velocity. Trade-offs: choosing Go means the on-call rotation needs Go expertise, and if we later need complex ORM-style domain modelling we are outside Go's strengths. Failure scenario: we pick Go for throughput, then the real requirement turns out to be heavy transactional domain logic with an existing team fluent in Spring — now we are paying a language-learning tax for throughput we did not need. Prevention: state the bottleneck and the constraint that drives the choice before committing, and validate the throughput assumption with a load test on a realistic handler in week one rather than trusting a hello-world benchmark. Alternative: Node, if the service is thin and the constraint is delivery speed rather than concurrency."

topics.description: Naming: the rules that make code readable within OOP, SOLID and Clean Code.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Why naming is architecture
The eight rules that matter, with the smell each one prevents

Names say what something *is*, not what it *does*. "What it does" belongs in the body; "what it is" belongs in the name. processOrderData() is a smell — processing what, how, and why is data? Prefer settleInvoice(). Exception: commands/functions legitimately describe the action (placeOrder, retryPendingCharges).

Booleans read as predicates, and positive names are safer. isActive, hasCapacity, shouldRetry, canRefund. Avoid double negatives (isNotDisabled) and avoid names that invite the wrong call: deleteQuietly (does it delete?), close() (does it free resources?).

is/has/can/should are conventions, not rules. Pick a convention for booleans in your codebase and apply it; the value is that a reader can scan a long boolean expression (if (a && !b && c)) without looking up each identifier.

Units and formats are in the name or they are in the type. timeoutMs not timeout, retryCount not retries (plural suggests a collection), amountMinor not amount, placedAt/expiresAt (timestamps as At, durations as a suffix: durationMs, intervalSec). This one rule prevents the most common class of production bug (seconds vs milliseconds).
Collections are plural, singular is one item. order, orders, orderIds. Distinguish user (the entity) from userId (the reference) from userRepository. The Id suffix is non-negotiable in TypeScript.

Distinguish the entity from the DTO from the command from the view. Same domain concept, four names, four layers: Order (domain), OrderRow (persistence), PlaceOrder (input command), OrderView (API output). If all four are Order, then every function that takes an Order must be checked for which one it really wanted. This is a real, common, expensive bug source.

get means retrieval; find means retrieval that can fail to find; load means retrieval that does I/O; create means construction that may or may not persist. These conventions are worth having because they answer "can this return null?" at the call site without reading the body:

Domain language over technical language, consistently. If the business says "fulfilment" and the code says shipment, every conversation requires a translation. If the code says "cancel" and the business says "void", same problem. Choose one and never mix — the biggest offender is a codebase with delete/remove/destroy meaning the same thing.
Additional high-value rules

Inconsistent synonyms for one concept across the codebase.
Boolean parameters: send(to, html, true, false) — four positional arguments and zero information. Use an options object with named booleans.

The rule
Ports and adapters, precisely
A port is an interface owned by the *inside*, expressed in domain language, describing what the inside needs. OrderRepository, PaymentGateway, Clock, NotificationSender.
An adapter is an implementation of a port that lives *outside* and knows the technology. SqlOrderRepository, StripePaymentGateway, SystemClock, SmtpNotificationSender.
A driving adapter (primary/hexagon side) takes input from outside and calls the application: HTTP controller, CLI command, message consumer, cron job.
A driven adapter (secondary side) is called by the application: database, message broker, HTTP client, filesystem.
The one-line test to state in an interview
Full worked example: place an order, hexagonal

topics.description: An anemic domain model consists of data-carrying classes with getters/setters and all behaviour in a separate service layer. It is the default outcome of naive layering, and it is the most common criticism of "clean architecture".
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The four costs of anemic models, stated precisely
Invalid states are representable. Any combination of fields is assignable. The compiler will not stop you, so the check happens in some service you forgot about.
Invariant duplication and drift. The same rule appears in every service that touches the entity; one of them will be out of date.
"Transaction script" sprawl. Services become scripts that do many things each, and each service can be entered from a different starting state.
The model cannot be reused. The next use case (a CLI, a scheduled job, a webhook) re-implements the rules differently, and now the rules exist four times.
An anemic model is the right choice when
The entity is mostly data with almost no invariants. A UserProfile, an AuditLogEntry, a Product in a catalogue: behaviour is CRUD and any "logic" is a projection. A rich model here is ceremony.
The logic is fundamentally about coordination, not about a single entity's invariants: an ETL job, an import/export pipeline, an API gateway, an orchestrator.
The domain is CRUD and the interesting complexity is in the UI or the queries. Content management, an admin panel, a simple catalogue.
The data is shared and write-heavy from many angles, and the "rules" are actually access rules → then your rules belong in the schema (constraints, permissions) and a service, not in a domain class.
You are serving a machine consumer, not a human. Anemic DTOs + a validation library is exactly right.

tradeoffs: *Rich models:* more code, higher initial cost, behaviour discoverable on the entity, invariants enforced once, reuse across entry points. *Anemic:* fast to write, trivially serialisable, ORM-friendly, trivially flat to reason about, but invariants are duplicated and can be violated by a new call path.

topics.title: Event-driven
topics.description: An architecture where components communicate by publishing and consuming events through a broker, so that the *timing and existence* of other components is not part of any component's knowledge. The unit of communication is a *fact that happened*, not a *request to do something*.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Three coupling kinds, and EDA reduces only one of them
What you gain
New consumers without producer changes. The most concrete gain: adding an analytics consumer requires zero changes to the producer.
Fan-out with independent failure and retry. A slow or broken consumer does not affect the producer (it affects only its own lag).
Independent scaling and deployment of consumers.
A durable audit/replay log — you can rebuild read models, debug from history, and implement "what if" analysis on real events.
Loose coupling in time, which enables buffering for spikes.
What you pay — and the honest list
Eventual consistency becomes visible to users. "Your order is processing" instead of "your order was placed". You now need a status model with intermediate states and a UI that communicates them.
You lose the ability to read the flow. In a choreographed design the sequence of steps lives in no single place. The flow *moves*, it does not disappear.
Debugging requires correlation. Every message needs traceparent, correlationId, causationId, and eventId; without them, incident response is archaeology.
commonMistakes: Publishing outside the transaction (the dual-write bug).
Non-idempotent consumers.
Events named as commands ("SendWelcomeEmail") — then the flow is invisible and a missing handler is silent.
Renaming/repurposing an event type.
No DLQ, no lag alerting.
Assuming exactly-once.
Replaying events into side-effecting handlers (duplicate emails, duplicate charges).

topics.title: Peer-to-peer
topics.description: Systems where nodes are peers with no central authority: they discover each other, coordinate, and replicate state directly. The two families that matter are content-addressable / decentralised data (blockchains, IPFS, Dynamo-style tables) and content-addressable systems more broadly (Fluentd, Bazel remote caching, Merkle trees, Merkle-DAGs, CRDT libraries).
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Two families, distinguished by what is decentralised
A. Coordination/P2P messaging and state
Gossip protocol: each node periodically exchanges state with a few random peers; information spreads in O(log n) rounds. Used by Cassandra, HashiCorp's memberlist, service discovery.

CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types): data structures whose merge is commutative, associative, and idempotent, so replicas converge without coordination. Types you should know: G-Counter (grow-only counter), PN-Counter, G-Set, OR-Set (observed-remove), LWW-Register, RGA/Logoot for sequences.
Vector clocks / hybrid logical clocks: per-replica versions to detect whether two writes are concurrent (conflict) or ordered (no conflict). Used by Dynamo.

Timestamps/ordering problem: there is no global clock. Solutions: physical clocks (unreliable), vector clocks (accurate, grows), hybrid logical clocks (drift-bounded, compact), Lamport clocks (causal order only).
B. Consensus and shared ledgers
The Byzantine Generals Problem: nodes may be malicious or faulty, so consensus must tolerate *arbitrary* faults, not just crashes. Practical Byzantine fault tolerance (pBFT) and its descendants.

Permissioned vs permissionless: whether nodes are known/allowed (permissioned: BFT with a known set, high throughput) or open (permissionless: probabilistic finality via Nakamoto consensus, open membership).
Probabilistic vs absolute finality: Bitcoin/Bitcoin-like chains give high-probability finality with a fork risk; BFT systems give deterministic finality with a known validator set.
The blockchain trilemma: decentralisation, security, and scalability — at most two, with Layer 2/off-chain channels/rollups as the practical escape.
commonMistakes: Confusing Dynamo-style quorum replication (not blockchain) with a ledger.
Assuming a CRDT is free — metadata, growth, and subtle semantics bugs are the price.
Choosing a blockchain where an audit log and a signature would do.
Ignoring conflict *semantics*: CRDTs converge the data structure; they cannot resolve "which of these two business decisions is correct".
Assuming availability without dealing with peer discovery and connectivity.

topics.title: CQRS
topics.description: Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate the write model (which enforces invariants and is optimised for consistency) from the read model (which is shaped for the query being served and optimised for read throughput). They may be the same process and the same database — the separation is logical before it is physical.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The honest threshold — when is a separate read model worth it?
Worth it when
The read:write ratio is high (typically >10:1) and reads are expensive (multi-join aggregations, sorting, full-text search).
The query shape differs fundamentally from the write shape (a dashboard aggregating 5 entities; a search over denormalised text).
Reads must scale or be geographically distributed separately from writes.
You are serving multiple distinct view requirements (mobile list vs admin detail vs export).
Reads need a different storage technology (full-text search, graph, columnar analytics).
You have a real CQRS framework or a project team that can operate the projection.
Not worth it when
The domain is CRUD and queries are 2-3 indexed lookups. You have added a projection to maintain, a lag to reason about, and a repair job to write.
One team, small scale, low traffic. Most systems never need CQRS.
commonMistakes: Starting at level 3 because it is "proper CQRS".
Reading from the read model inside a command.
No rebuild/repair capability.
No read-your-writes strategy, so users see ghost bugs.
Schema changes that require coordinated, non-backwards-compatible deploys across both models.
Projection lag unmonitored — discovered by customers.

topics.title: Event sourcing
topics.description: Event sourcing persists the sequence of domain events as the source of truth, and derives current state by replaying them. The event log is the system of record; "state" is a projection/cache.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
What you get (these are real and each is worth money)
Complete history. You can answer "what was this order's state on 12 March, at 14:03, and why?" — trivially and exactly. No other design gives you this.
Temporal queries. "Reconstruct the portfolio as of any past date." This is a genuine capability for finance, insurance, gaming, and anything with reporting obligations.
Rebuild any projection. Fix a bug in a read model: replay the log and rebuild it correctly. Change the projection logic; no data migration.
Event-driven integration. The log *is* the event stream — no dual-write problem for consumers, no outbox needed (the log is already durable and ordered per aggregate).
Debugging and support. You can replay a customer's history exactly. Support and fraud teams genuinely use this.
Fine-grained domain events with no impedance mismatch to the storage schema.
Natural optimistic concurrency via the aggregate version/sequence number.
What it costs (state these with equal fluency)

You must get the event schema right, and it is forever. Event 1 in 2024 is immutable in 2044. Events are not rows in a table you can UPDATE; they are the historical record. Every event must be self-contained (no "the price was the old value" — include the value), and every field addition must be backwards compatible forever.

Event upcasting is mandatory work. Old events need to be interpreted by new code. You need an upcaster chain (v1 → v2 → v3) from day one, and you need to write them and test them. Most teams underestimate this by an order of magnitude.
commonMistakes: No upcaster chain from day one — then year two is a rewrite.
Non-deterministic handlers; replay produces different state.

Deleting the projection and replaying during an incident, discovering the replay does not reproduce the current state (because someone mutated data directly). Prevention: projections are rebuildable by construction; never hand-edit them.
Putting side effects in the event handler (sending emails during replay → customers get 500 emails).
Underestimating the reporting/analytics requirement.
Treating events as a log you can edit.

topics.title: Hexagonal
topics.description: Clean Architecture (Uncle Bob, 2012) and Hexagonal Architecture (Alistair Cockburn, 2004) are the same idea: the domain is at the centre and depends on nothing; everything else is an adapter plugged into a port. The dependency arrow always points inward. Testability and technology independence come free.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The rule
Ports and adapters, precisely
A port is an interface owned by the *inside*, expressed in domain language, describing what the inside needs. OrderRepository, PaymentGateway, Clock, NotificationSender.
An adapter is an implementation of a port that lives *outside* and knows the technology. SqlOrderRepository, StripePaymentGateway, SystemClock, SmtpNotificationSender.
A driving adapter (primary/hexagon side) takes input from outside and calls the application: HTTP controller, CLI command, message consumer, cron job.
A driven adapter (secondary side) is called by the application: database, message broker, HTTP client, filesystem.
The one-line test to state in an interview
Full worked example: place an order, hexagonal
Why it is worth the cost (the actual benefits, not the aesthetics)
The domain is testable with zero infrastructure. Order.place(...) is a pure function; the whole domain test suite runs in milliseconds with no DB. This is the single most concrete, measurable payoff.
The use cases are testable with fake adapters — a FakePaymentGateway that declines on the third call is 10 lines and lets you test the decline path, which you can never test against real Stripe.

topics.title: BFF (backend for frontend)
topics.description: A Backend For Frontend is a service layer per client channel (web, mobile, TV, watch) that aggregates, reshapes, and adapts backend APIs into exactly the payload and endpoint shape that client needs. It is owned by the client team.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The problem it solves

API aggregation / fan-out. A product page needs product + price + inventory + reviews + recommendations. The client would make 5 calls, each with latency, each needing its own error handling, each exposing the internal API shape. A BFF makes 1 call.

Client-specific payload shaping. A web page needs 40 fields; a mobile app needs 8 for the same screen; a smart TV needs 4 in a different shape. One "universal" API forces every client to over-fetch and then ignore fields.
Encapsulation of service topology. When the pricing service is split in two, only the BFF changes — clients never learn about internal service decomposition.
A real BFF
The four design rules for a BFF that stay clean

No business rules. A BFF composes and reshapes; it does not decide prices, eligibility, or entitlements. Business rules live in the owning services. (The one exception: *presentation* rules — currency formatting, label selection, sort order for this channel — which are legitimately the BFF's job.)
It is per channel, not per screen. A BFF per screen produces dozens of tiny deployables with duplicated logic. A BFF per channel (web / mobile) produces 2–3 things.

It may cache aggressively; the backing services may not know about it. The BFF is the right place for a short-TTL aggregate cache and for request coalescing (join concurrent identical requests — single-flight).
It owns the error-to-UI mapping. An upstream 500 becomes a field-level "unavailable" plus a metric, not a blank page.
When a BFF is worth it (and when it is one service too many)
commonMistakes: Business rules creeping into the BFF (discount logic, eligibility).
A BFF per screen.
Sequential fan-out ("I need the product before I know which reviews to fetch") — usually avoidable.
No per-field fallback, so one slow service blanks the page.
Duplicated logic across web and mobile BFFs, then the two disagree.
Inventing data on failure.

topics.title: Service mesh awareness
topics.description: A service mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer (data plane + control plane) that handles service-to-service communication: mutual TLS, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, rate limiting, traffic splitting/shifting, telemetry, and authorisation policies — configured as configuration rather than embedded in code.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The two planes, precisely

Data plane: a sidecar proxy (Envoy, Linkerd2-proxy, Cilium) or a node-level/gateway proxy that sits on every request path and applies the policy. It is in the hot path of every request, which is why its performance and failure modes matter.
Control plane: pushes configuration to the data plane (xDS), manages certificates, aggregates telemetry, and provides the API you configure policies through.
What it gives you (this is the honest value list)

Uniform mTLS everywhere with automated certificate rotation. This is the single most-cited real benefit: mTLS between every service, with identity-based authorisation, without touching application code.

Retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, outlier detection, rate limits as declarative config — consistent across all services, including services written in languages you would not want to implement this in.

Traffic management: canary by percentage, header-based routing, mirroring (shadow traffic!), fault injection (inject delays/errors between two services on purpose). Canary without redeploys is a real, hard-won capability.
Uniform telemetry: consistent traceparent propagation, RED metrics (rate, errors, duration) per hop, and topology graphs that come for free.
Language/framework independence for cross-cutting concerns — a Node service and a Go service get identical retry behaviour.
Authorisation moved to infrastructure: identity-based policies (only service A may call B), reducing the need for bespoke auth code.

Latency and resource cost. Two hops per request (source sidecar → destination sidecar), extra CPU, extra memory per pod. For small packets the overhead is a real percentage of your p99; teams measure 1–3ms added p99 and extra node memory.
commonMistakes: Adopting a mesh with 6 services and one platform engineer.
Retrying in both the mesh and the client.
Retrying POSTs in the mesh.
Forgetting to configure holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts and wondering why pods get no traffic.
Mesh config edited by hand in the console with no review.
Treating the mesh as a security boundary for authorisation of *business* permissions (it authorises *service identity*, not "can this user refund").

topics.title: Monolith-to-microservices decision criteria
topics.description: Monolith-to-microservices decision criteria within Architectural Styles.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The prerequisite gate — do not skip this
The monolith's problem is code quality (no module boundaries, no tests, a God object). → Do modular-monolith work (11.3.2).
The monolith is fine; you just want to look modern. → Stop.
Requirements are still moving and you do not yet know the domains. → Wait; premature decomposition locks in wrong boundaries and is very hard to undo.
Criterion 1 — Change/deploy coupling
Measure: commits per module per month, deploy frequency, and the number of releases that carry changes to unrelated modules.
Threshold: ≥3 deployable components whose change rates differ by an order of magnitude, and a release train that couples them.
Evidence to gather: "we batch deploys monthly because of the billing change freeze" is the strongest single sentence you can bring to this conversation.
Criterion 2 — Scaling profile
Measure: CPU/memory/IO per endpoint, and what the cost of scaling the whole system is.
Threshold: one component consumes >50% of capacity while contributing <10% of revenue; or a component needs a different instance type/GPU/region than the rest.
commonMistakes: No prerequisites check, so you extract a badly-modelled domain and get a distributed monolith.
Extracting by technical layer rather than business capability.
Extracting the write path first.
Skipping step 0 (module boundary) and therefore having nothing clean to extract.
Extracting 5 services at once and learning nothing from the first.
Never deleting the old path, so you now maintain two systems forever.
Using the scorecard as a checkbox rather than measuring.

topics.title: Monolith: the default that is usually correct
topics.description: A single deployable unit containing all business logic, with internal layering (or none). "Monolith" describes the *deployment*, not the *code*: a well-structured monolith with hexagonal boundaries can be cleaner and more maintainable than a suite of microservices, and a tangled monolith is unmaintainable either way.
keyConcepts: Difficulty

Transactional integrity. Inside one process, one database transaction spans everything. Across services you get sagas, eventual consistency, and compensation — all strictly more expensive and strictly weaker.

Refactoring across the whole system. Change a field, and in a monolith you change it and the compiler finds every usage. Across services you change a schema and orchestrate N deploys with backwards compatibility for weeks.
Debugging. One process, one stack trace, one debugger, one log stream. Across services you need distributed tracing and you will still be guessing half the time.
Local development and deployment. One clone, one command, one deploy. The cost of microservices here is not just time; it is *feedback loop length*, which compounds with everything else.
What you actually gain by going to microservices
Independent deployment of components that change at different rates (a recommendation engine weekly vs. core billing monthly).
Independent scaling of components with different load profiles (search receiving 90% of traffic; batch jobs needing CPU not IOPS).
Technology heterogeneity where genuinely justified (a ML inference service in Python).
Fault isolation and blast-radius control for genuinely risky work.
Team autonomy and ownership alignment at scale (Conway's law in reverse).
Failure semantics you control — you can choose what is unavailable.
commonMistakes: Using "monolith" as an insult, which makes it a rhetorical position rather than a technical one.
Refusing to split at all even when a real, measured trigger appears (then you build a custom platform instead — usually worse).
Splitting along technical lines (a "database service", a "validation service") instead of business capabilities.
Treating "monolith" as "no structure". Unstructured monoliths cannot be extracted from.

tradeoffs: *"The monolith optimises for changeability and correctness; microservices optimise for independent scaling and team autonomy, at the cost of correctness guarantees and operational complexity."*

topics.title: Layered architecture and where it leaks
topics.description: Classic three-tier (Presentation → Business/Service → Data Access) or N-tier. Strictly ordered dependencies: each layer may call only the layer directly below it.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
What it gets right
Predictable navigation. "Where does the logic live?" has one answer.
Testable in principle: the service layer can be tested with a faked data layer.
Changeable in one direction: you can replace the database without touching the service layer (in theory — see below).
Simple to teach and to enforce, including with static analysis.

The service layer becomes anemic (11.2.9). All the logic is in services, entities are data bags, invariants are duplicated across services. This is the classic outcome of "service layer" as "all the methods".
The data layer leaks upward. The moment a service imports pg, or calls repo.queryBuilder(), or knows a column name, the boundary is gone. Symptom: import { db } from './data/db' in a service file.

The presentation layer leaks downward. Business logic in a controller: if (user.isVip) total *= 0.9. Now the same rule is not applied by the background job, because the job does not go through the controller. This is the single most common real bug in layered systems.

Transactions leak upward. Services need "one transaction across these three repositories"; if each repository manages its own transaction, you cannot compose. The fix pushes transaction demarcation *up* to an application layer above the services.
The presentation layer contains domain rules that are also duplicated elsewhere. Same as 3 but for cross-cutting rules (validation, authorisation, status transitions).

Shared-nothing layers become "shared-everything" layers. When two services need the same helper, it goes into a common layer. Then everyone imports common, and common imports everything (it needed one thing from each layer). This is the "layer cake turned inside out" and it is the beginning of the death of the architecture.
commonMistakes: common / utils / helpers layer that everything imports.
Entities that are ORM models, so the data layer's types are everywhere.
Business rules in controllers (and nowhere else).
Layer-first folder structure in a codebase with many features.
"Strictly layered" enforced only by convention.
Anemic services (which is the *definition* of the naive service layer).

tradeoffs: *Gain:* simple, enforceable, familiar, easy to test with a faked data layer, easy to navigate.

```
│ Presentation (controllers, UI, HTTP) │  ← knows about the service layer only
├──────────────────────────────────────┤
```

```
src/

```

topics.title: Microservices: what you actually gain and lose
topics.description: An architecture where an application is decomposed into many small, independently deployable services, each owning its data, communicating over the network, usually organised around business capabilities.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The honest framing, which you should open with in an interview

Independent deployability of differently-changing components. If the recommendation service changes weekly and billing changes monthly, a shared release train makes the weekly work wait for the monthly risk. This is the strongest argument and it is organisational, not technical.
Independent scaling. Different resource profiles: search is IO- and memory-heavy; inference is GPU-heavy; checkout is bursty. Scaling one without the others is the real financial argument.
Failure isolation for risky work. A new ML service can be wrong without endangering the payment path. Also regulatory/data-isolation boundaries (PCI scope, PII residency, tenant isolation).
Everything else usually claimed is not a real benefit
The cost list, in the order an interview will probe it
Calls fail. Partial failure is the *normal* case, not the exception. Every call site needs: timeout, retry policy with jitter, idempotency, error taxonomy, and a decision about what the user sees.
No ACID across services. Enter eventual consistency: sagas, compensation, reconciliation, and a user-visible intermediate state.
Debugging requires infrastructure. Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry), log correlation with traceparent, and the discipline to propagate them. Without it you are guessing.

Data duplication and cross-service queries. "Show the order with its customer name and product names" becomes 3 API calls, a fan-out with a latency budget, or a denormalised read model (which then needs rebuilding).
Contract management. Every synchronous API is a distributed-system contract that must be versioned, backward compatible, tested (consumer-driven contract tests), and monitored.
commonMistakes: Extracting by technical layer (an "auth service", a "validation service") rather than business capability.
Sharing the database while claiming data ownership.
Sync-everything with no idempotency or timeout.
Assuming "we will add tracing next quarter".
Treating the service count as an architecture metric.
No platform/ops investment.

tradeoffs: *Microservices trade transactional correctness and operational simplicity for independent deployment, independent scaling, and fault isolation — and the trade only pays at a certain team and product scale.*

topics.title: Event-driven architecture: coupling, consistency, and failure handling
topics.description: An architecture where components communicate by publishing and consuming events through a broker, so that the *timing and existence* of other components is not part of any component's knowledge. The unit of communication is a *fact that happened*, not a *request to do something*.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Three coupling kinds, and EDA reduces only one of them
What you gain
New consumers without producer changes. The most concrete gain: adding an analytics consumer requires zero changes to the producer.
Fan-out with independent failure and retry. A slow or broken consumer does not affect the producer (it affects only its own lag).
Independent scaling and deployment of consumers.
A durable audit/replay log — you can rebuild read models, debug from history, and implement "what if" analysis on real events.
Loose coupling in time, which enables buffering for spikes.
What you pay — and the honest list
Eventual consistency becomes visible to users. "Your order is processing" instead of "your order was placed". You now need a status model with intermediate states and a UI that communicates them.
You lose the ability to read the flow. In a choreographed design the sequence of steps lives in no single place. The flow *moves*, it does not disappear.
Debugging requires correlation. Every message needs traceparent, correlationId, causationId, and eventId; without them, incident response is archaeology.
commonMistakes: Publishing outside the transaction (the dual-write bug).
Non-idempotent consumers.
Events named as commands ("SendWelcomeEmail") — then the flow is invisible and a missing handler is silent.
Renaming/repurposing an event type.
No DLQ, no lag alerting.
Assuming exactly-once.
Replaying events into side-effecting handlers (duplicate emails, duplicate charges).

tradeoffs: One sentence: *EDA removes temporal and deployment coupling at the cost of immediate consistency, flow visibility, and operational and schema-governance complexity.*

topics.title: CQRS: when a separate read model is worth it
topics.description: Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate the write model (which enforces invariants and is optimised for consistency) from the read model (which is shaped for the query being served and optimised for read throughput). They may be the same process and the same database — the separation is logical before it is physical.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The honest threshold — when is a separate read model worth it?
Worth it when
The read:write ratio is high (typically >10:1) and reads are expensive (multi-join aggregations, sorting, full-text search).
The query shape differs fundamentally from the write shape (a dashboard aggregating 5 entities; a search over denormalised text).
Reads must scale or be geographically distributed separately from writes.
You are serving multiple distinct view requirements (mobile list vs admin detail vs export).
Reads need a different storage technology (full-text search, graph, columnar analytics).
You have a real CQRS framework or a project team that can operate the projection.
Not worth it when
The domain is CRUD and queries are 2-3 indexed lookups. You have added a projection to maintain, a lag to reason about, and a repair job to write.
One team, small scale, low traffic. Most systems never need CQRS.
commonMistakes: Starting at level 3 because it is "proper CQRS".
Reading from the read model inside a command.
No rebuild/repair capability.
No read-your-writes strategy, so users see ghost bugs.
Schema changes that require coordinated, non-backwards-compatible deploys across both models.
Projection lag unmonitored — discovered by customers.

topics.title: Event sourcing: the honest trade-off
topics.description: Event sourcing persists the sequence of domain events as the source of truth, and derives current state by replaying them. The event log is the system of record; "state" is a projection/cache.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
What you get (these are real and each is worth money)
Complete history. You can answer "what was this order's state on 12 March, at 14:03, and why?" — trivially and exactly. No other design gives you this.
Temporal queries. "Reconstruct the portfolio as of any past date." This is a genuine capability for finance, insurance, gaming, and anything with reporting obligations.
Rebuild any projection. Fix a bug in a read model: replay the log and rebuild it correctly. Change the projection logic; no data migration.
Event-driven integration. The log *is* the event stream — no dual-write problem for consumers, no outbox needed (the log is already durable and ordered per aggregate).
Debugging and support. You can replay a customer's history exactly. Support and fraud teams genuinely use this.
Fine-grained domain events with no impedance mismatch to the storage schema.
Natural optimistic concurrency via the aggregate version/sequence number.
What it costs (state these with equal fluency)

You must get the event schema right, and it is forever. Event 1 in 2024 is immutable in 2044. Events are not rows in a table you can UPDATE; they are the historical record. Every event must be self-contained (no "the price was the old value" — include the value), and every field addition must be backwards compatible forever.

Event upcasting is mandatory work. Old events need to be interpreted by new code. You need an upcaster chain (v1 → v2 → v3) from day one, and you need to write them and test them. Most teams underestimate this by an order of magnitude.
commonMistakes: No upcaster chain from day one — then year two is a rewrite.
Non-deterministic handlers; replay produces different state.

Deleting the projection and replaying during an incident, discovering the replay does not reproduce the current state (because someone mutated data directly). Prevention: projections are rebuildable by construction; never hand-edit them.
Putting side effects in the event handler (sending emails during replay → customers get 500 emails).
Underestimating the reporting/analytics requirement.
Treating events as a log you can edit.

tradeoffs: *Event sourcing buys perfect history, replay, and temporal queries at the cost of immutable forever-schemas, mandatory upcasting, projection infrastructure, lost ad-hoc querying, and a real conflict with erasure requirements.*

topics.title: Serverless architecture: constraints and the function-per-request trap
topics.description: Run your application as small, stateless, short-lived units ("functions") invoked by events, with all state and durable coordination in managed services. The *operational* model (you manage the code; the platform manages the infrastructure) is the actual essence; "no servers" is marketing.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The four real constraints — know these and the design follows

Cold starts and connection reuse. A cold start means: allocate a sandbox, download code, initialise the runtime, run your module-level code. Your module-level code (a DB pool, an HTTP agent, a big require) runs on *every* invocation in some runtimes and *occasionally* in others. Mitigations: minimise module-level work, keep the package small, use provisioned concurrency, keep the handler at the top level of the file, reuse clients via module scope (or a global, which survives warm invocations).
Execution timeouts (15 min hard cap on major platforms; far less for your HTTP timeout). This is the hard boundary on any long-running work.

Concurrency and burst limits. Thousands of concurrent invocations; you will hit account concurrency limits and per-function limits. This means every connection pool must be sized for the worst-case concurrent invocation count, and a DB will see a thundering herd.

State must be external. No in-memory state survives reliably; no sticky sessions; no local disk. Everything durable in DynamoDB/S3/Postgres/etc. Ephemeral /tmp may exist but is not durable and is not shared.
The function-per-request trap
The three serverless architectures, and which trap each avoids
Cold start anatomy and the optimisations that actually matter
Concurrency model: the under-appreciated constraint
Reduce concurrency (reserved concurrency per function, SQS with a low maxReceiveCount/visibility, or a serialising queue).
Use a proxy/pooler (RDS Proxy, PgBouncer transaction pooling).
commonMistakes: New connection pool per invocation → connection exhaustion at exactly the moment traffic spikes.
Function per route with a shared "utils" that opens everything.
Retrying an SQS message 5 times with no DLQ and no idempotency.
Failing an entire batch because one record failed.
No concurrency limit on a function that hammers a fragile dependency.
Long-running work in a function.
Assuming the function is stateless-and-therefore-fast: cold start is not free.

tradeoffs: *Gain:* no server management, elastic scaling, per-invocation cost, fine-grained deploys, and pay-for-idle near zero for spiky workloads.

topics.title: BFF
topics.description: A Backend For Frontend is a service layer per client channel (web, mobile, TV, watch) that aggregates, reshapes, and adapts backend APIs into exactly the payload and endpoint shape that client needs. It is owned by the client team.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The problem it solves

API aggregation / fan-out. A product page needs product + price + inventory + reviews + recommendations. The client would make 5 calls, each with latency, each needing its own error handling, each exposing the internal API shape. A BFF makes 1 call.

Client-specific payload shaping. A web page needs 40 fields; a mobile app needs 8 for the same screen; a smart TV needs 4 in a different shape. One "universal" API forces every client to over-fetch and then ignore fields.
Encapsulation of service topology. When the pricing service is split in two, only the BFF changes — clients never learn about internal service decomposition.
A real BFF
The four design rules for a BFF that stay clean

No business rules. A BFF composes and reshapes; it does not decide prices, eligibility, or entitlements. Business rules live in the owning services. (The one exception: *presentation* rules — currency formatting, label selection, sort order for this channel — which are legitimately the BFF's job.)
It is per channel, not per screen. A BFF per screen produces dozens of tiny deployables with duplicated logic. A BFF per channel (web / mobile) produces 2–3 things.

It may cache aggressively; the backing services may not know about it. The BFF is the right place for a short-TTL aggregate cache and for request coalescing (join concurrent identical requests — single-flight).
It owns the error-to-UI mapping. An upstream 500 becomes a field-level "unavailable" plus a metric, not a blank page.
When a BFF is worth it (and when it is one service too many)
commonMistakes: Business rules creeping into the BFF (discount logic, eligibility).
A BFF per screen.
Sequential fan-out ("I need the product before I know which reviews to fetch") — usually avoidable.
No per-field fallback, so one slow service blanks the page.
Duplicated logic across web and mobile BFFs, then the two disagree.
Inventing data on failure.

tradeoffs: *Gain:* fewer round trips, smaller payloads, per-channel agility, topology encapsulation, clean degradation, and independent client-team deploys.

topics.title: Peer-to-peer architectures awareness
topics.description: Systems where nodes are peers with no central authority: they discover each other, coordinate, and replicate state directly. The two families that matter are content-addressable / decentralised data (blockchains, IPFS, Dynamo-style tables) and content-addressable systems more broadly (Fluentd, Bazel remote caching, Merkle trees, Merkle-DAGs, CRDT libraries).
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Two families, distinguished by what is decentralised
A. Coordination/P2P messaging and state
Gossip protocol: each node periodically exchanges state with a few random peers; information spreads in O(log n) rounds. Used by Cassandra, HashiCorp's memberlist, service discovery.

CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types): data structures whose merge is commutative, associative, and idempotent, so replicas converge without coordination. Types you should know: G-Counter (grow-only counter), PN-Counter, G-Set, OR-Set (observed-remove), LWW-Register, RGA/Logoot for sequences.
Vector clocks / hybrid logical clocks: per-replica versions to detect whether two writes are concurrent (conflict) or ordered (no conflict). Used by Dynamo.

Timestamps/ordering problem: there is no global clock. Solutions: physical clocks (unreliable), vector clocks (accurate, grows), hybrid logical clocks (drift-bounded, compact), Lamport clocks (causal order only).
B. Consensus and shared ledgers
The Byzantine Generals Problem: nodes may be malicious or faulty, so consensus must tolerate *arbitrary* faults, not just crashes. Practical Byzantine fault tolerance (pBFT) and its descendants.

Permissioned vs permissionless: whether nodes are known/allowed (permissioned: BFT with a known set, high throughput) or open (permissionless: probabilistic finality via Nakamoto consensus, open membership).
Probabilistic vs absolute finality: Bitcoin/Bitcoin-like chains give high-probability finality with a fork risk; BFT systems give deterministic finality with a known validator set.
The blockchain trilemma: decentralisation, security, and scalability — at most two, with Layer 2/off-chain channels/rollups as the practical escape.
commonMistakes: Confusing Dynamo-style quorum replication (not blockchain) with a ledger.
Assuming a CRDT is free — metadata, growth, and subtle semantics bugs are the price.
Choosing a blockchain where an audit log and a signature would do.
Ignoring conflict *semantics*: CRDTs converge the data structure; they cannot resolve "which of these two business decisions is correct".
Assuming availability without dealing with peer discovery and connectivity.

topics.title: Choosing a style: the decision framework and how to defend it
topics.description: Choosing a style: the decision framework and how to defend it within Architectural Styles.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
The decision matrix
How to defend it — the eight arguments that land

"Start with the monolith and split later" is a trap; start with the *modular* monolith." The extraction cost is determined by the quality of the internal boundaries. If you have enforced module boundaries and data ownership, extraction is weeks; without them, it is months.

"Splitting a system along business capabilities is the only defensible split." Splitting by technical layer (an auth service, a validation service, a logging service) creates the distributed monolith: everything must deploy together anyway, and you have all the costs of distribution.

"The real cost of microservices is the loss of a transaction and a debugger, not the network." One ACID transaction spanning a change is worth more than most read-traffic arguments. Sagas are strictly weaker: partial states, compensation logic, reconciliation jobs, and a support burden.

"Team size is the strongest predictor, and the rule of thumb is that a service needs 2+ teams' worth of ownership to be worth the operational cost." Below one team per service you get all the costs and none of the benefit.
"Read and write patterns are the second most common justification, and CQRS addresses it without microservices." You can get a separate read model inside a monolith. Do that before you distribute.

"Operational maturity is a hard prerequisite." Distributed tracing, on-call, automated deployment with rollback, and a platform team. Without these, microservices convert application bugs into platform incidents.

"Every service boundary you add creates a distributed systems problem you now own forever." Backward compatibility, contract tests, idempotency, retries, timeouts, and schema evolution — per boundary. Count them.
"You can reverse most of this; you cannot reverse a data model split." Data ownership is the irreversible part. Code extraction can be undone; a split database with cross-service joins cannot.
You have ≥8 teams with independent roadmaps blocked by a shared release train.
commonMistakes: Answering "it depends" with no criteria. Have the six questions ready.
Naming a style without a trigger metric.
Confusing deployment frequency with architecture.
Recommending microservices for a code-quality problem.
Forgetting to ask about operational maturity.
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```
1. What are the invariants, and do they span more than one store?
   → If yes: transaction boundaries matter. Lean toward fewer processes (monolith).
2. What is the read:write ratio, and do reads need shapes different from what writes produce?
   → If yes and measurably expensive: consider a read model (CQRS level 2).
3. What must scale independently, and can you MEASURE it?
   → If you can name a component with a disproportionate load profile: consider extracting it.
4. What changes at what rate, and what must deploy independently?
   → If components have order-of-magnitude-different change rates: consider services.
5. How many teams, and how do they coordinate today?
   → <5 teams: modular monolith. >5-8 with independent roadmaps: consider services.
6. What are the failure/consistency requirements, and what is your operational capacity?
   → High transactional consistency + low ops capacity: monolith. Isolated blast radius +
     strong ops capacity: services.
```

```
Start: a feature-first modular monolith with a thin shared kernel, ports at volatile boundaries,
      and a rich domain model where the complexity is.
Add:  a CQRS read projection for the specific read bottleneck you can measure.
Add:  in-process domain events; a broker only when you need replay or independent consumer scaling.
Extract: at most the one or two components with a measured scaling/deployment/team/isolation trigger.
Never: split because the requirements are unclear, because the code is messy, or because
       microservices are the fashionable answer.
```

topics.title: Elevator
topics.description: Elevator within Low-Level Design Case Studies.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Constraints
The car must not reverse direction while passengers are inside (or with pending requests behind it).
Doors must not open on an intermediate floor while travelling.
Request coalescing: multiple requests for the same floor → one stop.
Fairness: no starvation (a request far in the travel direction keeps being overtaken).
State and invariants
The tricky part

Fairness vs efficiency. SCAN is simple and efficient but starves far requests if traffic is asymmetric; a "collective control" with look-ahead (a scheduling algorithm that plans the whole set of trips) is the sophisticated answer. Name both, implement one.

Direction reversal rules. The interesting rule is: the car continues in its direction if there are passengers going that way, OR if there is a hall request in that direction; only then does it reverse. Getting this exactly right is worth more than anything else here.

The destination-dispatch (destination control) design is a genuinely different architecture: passengers enter and press a floor *before* the doors open, so the car knows its full manifest and can be scheduled globally (a group-controller / BFS-based scheduler). This is the "real" elevator algorithm and mentioning it shows depth.

Failure and safety: fire alarm overrides everything; a stuck door, a sensor fault, an over-speed governor. These belong in the state machine as transitions with priority, not in if statements in the tick loop.

topics.title: Splitwise
topics.description: Splitwise within Low-Level Design Case Studies.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Split modes: equally, exact amounts, percentages, shares/weights. Support multiple currencies.
Constraints
Balances must be computable incrementally (O(1) per expense) — recomputing from scratch is O(expenses × participants) and does not scale.
Rounding: 100 cents split 3 ways is 33.33 — you must define who gets the remainder and be consistent.
Money is never a float.
Simplification is a graph problem, not a pairwise loop.
State and invariants
The tricky part

Rounding and remainders. Must be deterministic and documented, and must sum exactly. The classic failure is 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 compounded across 100 expenses; the answer is integer minor units with a single documented remainder rule. Bonus: state that "always give the remainder to the same participant" can be exploited, so use a stable, non-collusion-prone tie-break.

Simplification minimality. Greedy (largest-first matching) is O(n log n) and produces at most n−1 transfers; it is *not* always the absolute minimum, and saying that shows depth. The exact minimum is a subset-sum problem; for small n, exhaustive search is feasible.

Multi-currency. You cannot convert balances without an FX rate, and the rate changes. The correct model: store each expense in the currency it was incurred in, and either (a) require a group currency and store the FX rate + timestamp per expense, or (b) compute per-currency balances separately and settle per currency. Do not silently use the current rate for a 6-month-old expense.

topics.description: Tic-tac-toe within Low-Level Design Case Studies.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Constraints
API surface + full implementation
State and invariants
The tricky part
Move ordering for alpha-beta effectiveness: try centre, then corners, then edges. In tic-tac-toe with a full tree this is fast enough that pruning is not needed; with a depth limit it matters.

Terminal position scoring with depth: 10 - depth for a win and -10 + depth for a loss, so the AI prefers winning *fast* and losing *slowly*. Without the depth term the AI is indifferent and makes silly moves.

Pruning correctness: you must return a score, not undefined, from a pruned node; and the alpha/beta update must be alpha = max(alpha, best) at MAX nodes and beta = min(beta, worst) at MIN nodes. A subtle bug here yields a *plausible but wrong* AI, which is hard to detect — property tests catch it.
Determinism: tie-break by lowest move index so the game is reproducible and tests are stable.

The generalisation: for larger boards (noughts and crosses, Connect-4, Go) you need negamax, transposition tables, move ordering heuristics, iterative deepening, and killer/history heuristics. Knowing these names, and that tic-tac-toe's full tree is only ~550k nodes with 9! ≈ 362,880 game sequences, is the depth signal.
Extension points
Ai interface: random, first-move, greedy, minimax(depth), minimax + alpha-beta, negamax + transposition table, MCTS (UCT), neural-net policy.

topics.title: Library management
topics.description: Library management within Low-Level Design Case Studies.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Constraints
A title (bibliographic record) vs a copy (physical item): one title, N copies; only a copy is borrowed.
Reservation queue ordering (FIFO, with an expiry window).
Borrowing limits per membership type and no-reservation-if-unavailable rules.

Concurrency: two members reserving the last copy simultaneously.
State and invariants
The tricky part

The availability/reservation race. Two members reserve the last copy. Solution: a unique constraint per (title, queue position) or a serialisable transaction / SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the title row, plus a uniqueness constraint on (copyId) for the active reservation. Interviewers like this because it combines a domain rule with a concurrency answer.

The reservation queue expiry vs fulfilment. On return, if there is a queue, the copy goes to 'reserved' and the next member is notified with a hold window; if they do not collect in time, the copy is released to the next. This is a second state machine inside a method — a common place to accidentally lose copies.

Renewal rules. Refuse renewal if reserved; refuse if there are no available copies of that title (an "awaiting pickup" nuance); cap renewals; and extend from the *current due date*, not from today (a classic bug).

topics.description: Tic-tac-toe with AI within Low-Level Design Case Studies.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Constraints
API surface + full implementation
State and invariants
The tricky part
Move ordering for alpha-beta effectiveness: try centre, then corners, then edges. In tic-tac-toe with a full tree this is fast enough that pruning is not needed; with a depth limit it matters.

Terminal position scoring with depth: 10 - depth for a win and -10 + depth for a loss, so the AI prefers winning *fast* and losing *slowly*. Without the depth term the AI is indifferent and makes silly moves.

Pruning correctness: you must return a score, not undefined, from a pruned node; and the alpha/beta update must be alpha = max(alpha, best) at MAX nodes and beta = min(beta, worst) at MIN nodes. A subtle bug here yields a *plausible but wrong* AI, which is hard to detect — property tests catch it.
Determinism: tie-break by lowest move index so the game is reproducible and tests are stable.

The generalisation: for larger boards (noughts and crosses, Connect-4, Go) you need negamax, transposition tables, move ordering heuristics, iterative deepening, and killer/history heuristics. Knowing these names, and that tic-tac-toe's full tree is only ~550k nodes with 9! ≈ 362,880 game sequences, is the depth signal.
Extension points
Ai interface: random, first-move, greedy, minimax(depth), minimax + alpha-beta, negamax + transposition table, MCTS (UCT), neural-net policy.

topics.title: Library management system
topics.description: Library management system within Low-Level Design Case Studies.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Constraints
A title (bibliographic record) vs a copy (physical item): one title, N copies; only a copy is borrowed.
Reservation queue ordering (FIFO, with an expiry window).
Borrowing limits per membership type and no-reservation-if-unavailable rules.
Overdue tracking and fee calculation; fines can block borrowing.
Concurrency: two members reserving the last copy simultaneously.
State and invariants
The tricky part

The availability/reservation race. Two members reserve the last copy. Solution: a unique constraint per (title, queue position) or a serialisable transaction / SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the title row, plus a uniqueness constraint on (copyId) for the active reservation. Interviewers like this because it combines a domain rule with a concurrency answer.

The reservation queue expiry vs fulfilment. On return, if there is a queue, the copy goes to 'reserved' and the next member is notified with a hold window; if they do not collect in time, the copy is released to the next. This is a second state machine inside a method — a common place to accidentally lose copies.

Renewal rules. Refuse renewal if reserved; refuse if there are no available copies of that title (an "awaiting pickup" nuance); cap renewals; and extend from the *current due date*, not from today (a classic bug).
